# Overview

cppDE generates and compiles C++ code per model: for ODE models through
\texttt{cppODE()} and \texttt{cvode()}, for algebraic models through
\texttt{cppFUN()} (Table \ref{tab:entry-points}).

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{@{} l l l l @{}}
\toprule
                  & \texttt{cppODE()}          & \texttt{cvode()}         & \texttt{cppFUN()}           \\
\midrule
problem           & ODE                        & ODE                      & algebraic $y = g(x, p)$     \\
\texttt{method}   & \texttt{bdf}, \texttt{adams}, \texttt{rb4}, \texttt{tsit5} & \texttt{bdf}, \texttt{adams} & none \\
first order       & forward, reverse           & forward, reverse         & forward, reverse            \\
second order      & forward-forward,           & none                     & forward-forward,            \\
                  & forward-reverse            &                          & forward-reverse             \\
derivatives       & dual numbers, adjoint      & forward sensitivity      & dual numbers                \\
                  &                            & equations                &                             \\
libraries         & LAPACK, KLU optional       & SUNDIALS $\ge 6.0$,      & none                        \\
                  &                            & KLU optional             &                             \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{The three entry points. All share the code generator of
Section \ref{sec:codegen}; the two integrators share
\texttt{solveODE()}.}
\label{tab:entry-points}
\end{table}

\texttt{cppODE()} and \texttt{cvode()} share their R interface: both
take named character vectors of right-hand sides with optional events,
forcings and parameter vectors and return a model handle for
\texttt{solveODE()}. They differ only in the numerical core.
\texttt{cppODE()} emits self-contained C++ that includes the headers
under \texttt{inst/include/cppde/}. \texttt{cvode()} emits glue code
that links the system-installed SUNDIALS CVODE/CVODES library and
inherits its numerical behaviour.

Section \ref{sec:codegen} describes the shared code generator.
Section \ref{sec:cppde} covers the in-tree integrator \texttt{cppODE()}:
four time-stepping methods, forward-mode automatic differentiation for
parameter sensitivities, the reverse-mode discrete adjoint, whose cost
does not depend on the number of parameters, and sensitivities across
events. Section \ref{sec:cvode} covers \texttt{cvode()} and its
adjoint sensitivity analysis, and Section \ref{sec:funcpp}
\texttt{cppFUN()}, used for observation maps and reparametrisations $p = \Phi(\theta)$.
Section \ref{sec:bench} benchmarks the two integrators against each
other on $43$ problems, and the reverse and second-order modes against
their forward counterparts.

# Code generation \label{sec:codegen}

Every entry point turns the user's expressions into straight-line C++
templated over the scalar type, so one source serves the value,
dual-number and nested-dual instantiations. The further derivatives the
integrators need are formed at code-generation time by automatic
differentiation [@griewank2008evaluating] on an expression graph: the
Jacobian, the contractions of the discrete adjoint, and the time
derivatives of the right-hand side and of the event roots.

\textbf{Expression graph.} Each expression is read by Python's own
parser and lowered into a directed acyclic graph with states, parameters,
forcings, time and constants as leaves and sums, products, powers and
function calls as inner nodes. Nodes are hash-consed
[@ershov1958programming; @filliatre2006hashconsing]: a node is
identified by its operation, operands and constant attributes and is
created at most once, so a repeated subexpression is a single node
without a separate elimination pass. Sums and products are kept flat
with numeric coefficients and exponents, and numeric constants are
normalised so that equal values map to equal nodes. Syntax the parser
does not read goes through SymPy into the same graph; SymPy also
supplies the derivative of a function the graph has no rule for.

\begin{figure}[h]
\centering
\begin{tikzpicture}[x=1.15cm, y=1.05cm, >=latex,
    op/.style={circle, draw, inner sep=1pt, minimum size=6mm},
    leaf/.style={inner sep=2pt}]
  \node[leaf] (k1) at (0, 0) {$k_1$};
  \node[leaf] (A)  at (1, 0) {$A$};
  \node[leaf] (B)  at (2, 0) {$B$};
  \node[leaf] (C)  at (3, 0) {$C$};
  \node[leaf] (k2) at (4, 0) {$k_2$};
  \node[op] (u) at (1, 1.3) {$\times$};
  \node[op] (v) at (3.5, 1.3) {$\times$};
  \node[op] (s) at (1.5, 2.6) {$+$};
  \node[op] (r) at (3, 2.6) {$+$};
  \node[leaf] (fs) at (1.5, 3.6) {$f_A,\ f_B$};
  \node[leaf] (fr) at (3, 3.6) {$f_C$};
  \foreach \a in {k1, A, B} \draw[->] (\a) -- (u);
  \foreach \a in {C, k2} \draw[->] (\a) -- (v);
  \draw[->] (u) -- node[left, font=\scriptsize] {$-1$} (s);
  \draw[->] (v) -- (s);
  \draw[->] (u) -- (r);
  \draw[->] (v) -- node[right, font=\scriptsize] {$-1$} (r);
  \draw[->] (s) -- (fs);
  \draw[->] (r) -- (fr);
\end{tikzpicture}
\caption{Expression graph of $f_A = f_B = -k_1 A B + k_2 C$ and
$f_C = k_1 A B - k_2 C$; edge labels are coefficients.}
\label{fig:expression-graph}
\end{figure}

\textbf{Example.} In Figure \ref{fig:expression-graph} each product is
one node, and so are the equal right-hand sides $f_A$ and $f_B$. Nodes
used more than once become temporaries:
\begin{verbatim}
const double _t0 = params[4]*x[2];       // k2*C
const double _t1 = params[3]*x[0]*x[1];  // k1*A*B
const double _t2 = _t0 - _t1;
dxdt[0] = _t2;
dxdt[1] = _t2;
dxdt[2] = -_t0 + _t1;
\end{verbatim}

\textbf{Derivatives.} A forward sweep over the graph forms a
Jacobian-vector product, a reverse sweep a vector-Jacobian product,
each in time linear in the size of the graph [@griewank2008evaluating].
Both add nodes to the same graph, so derivative and value share their
common parts. The reverse contractions $J^{\mathsf T}\lambda$ and
$(\partial f/\partial p)^{\mathsf T}\lambda$ are vector-Jacobian
products; the derivatives the Rosenbrock stages and the event
localisation require are Jacobian-vector products along $\dot x = f$.

The Jacobian $J = \partial f/\partial x$ is assembled by entries or by
colouring. By entries, each state-dependent node carries the
sparse gradient of its value with respect to the states, and the
gradients of the graph roots are the nonzero entries of $J$. The cost
of this accumulation,
$W_{\mathrm{ent}} = \sum_{v} |\mathrm{supp}\,\nabla v|$ summed over
the $E_s$ state-dependent nodes $v$ of $f$, grows with the density of
$J$. Entries are used while
$W_{\mathrm{ent}} \le \max(4E_s, 50\,000)$. Beyond that, a greedy
distance-2 colouring of the column intersection graph groups
structurally orthogonal columns
[@curtis1974estimation; @coleman1983estimation; @gebremedhin2005color].
If it needs at most $n_x/4$ colours, one Jacobian-vector product per
colour, seeded with ones on the columns of that colour, recovers those
columns; otherwise entries are kept.

\textbf{Linear tables.} A sum of at least twelve terms
$c_j\,x_j\,\varphi$ with numeric $c_j$ and a common state-free factor
$\varphi$ becomes a row of a constant matrix $C$, so that
$f(x) = \phi(x, Cx)$. The generated code evaluates $z = Cx$ once per
call from a sparse or dense table, and assembles the Jacobian as
\begin{equation}
  J = \frac{\partial \phi}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial \phi}{\partial z}\,C,
  \label{eq:linmap-jacobian}
\end{equation}
while the reverse contractions apply $C^{\mathsf T}$. A dense coupling,
such as a dipolar interaction among all states, thus costs a table
rather than a sum of expressions per entry.

\textbf{Loops.} Statements whose graphs agree up to state indices and
constants, such as those a method-of-lines discretisation repeats for
every grid point, form a class. A class of at least sixteen instances
is emitted as one loop over index and constant tables, and a sum of
many terms of one structure as an inner loop. Differentiation stays
per instance, so the work of the generator grows with the number of
instances, while the size of the emitted code for a regular model does
not.

# \texttt{cppODE()} \label{sec:cppde}

## Initial-value problem

\texttt{cppODE()} solves
\begin{equation}
  \dot{x}  = f\bigl(x,\, p_{\mathrm{dyn}},\, t\bigr),
  \qquad x(t_0) = p_{\mathrm{init}},
  \label{eq:ivp}
\end{equation}
with state $x \in \mathbb{R}^{n_x}$ and parameters
$p = (p_{\mathrm{init}}, p_{\mathrm{dyn}})$, the initial conditions and
the dynamic parameters. The right-hand side $f$
may depend explicitly on time (non-autonomous systems), as the
forcing functions that inject time-dependent inputs require.
$J = \partial f / \partial x$ denotes the state Jacobian throughout.
The coefficients of the four methods are listed in Appendices
\ref{app:bdf-coeffs} to \ref{app:tsit5-coeffs}.

## Stiffness and the choice of method

Stability is analysed on the linear test equation
$\dot y = \lambda y$, $\lambda \in \mathbb{C}^-$. A one-step method
multiplies $y$ by an amplification factor $R(z)$ per step,
$z = h \lambda$. The method is \emph{A-stable} if $|R(z)| \le 1$ on
the entire left half-plane, so that the numerical solution decays
whenever the exact one does, for any step size;
\emph{A($\alpha$)-stable} if the bound holds on the wedge
$\{ z \in \mathbb{C} : |\arg(-z)| \le \alpha \}$ for some
$\alpha < 90^{\circ}$; and \emph{L-stable} if it is A-stable and
$R(z) \to 0$ as $\operatorname{Re}(z) \to -\infty$, which damps very
stiff transients within one step.

Problem \eqref{eq:ivp} is \emph{stiff} on $[t_0, t_{\mathrm{end}}]$
when an explicit method must take steps much smaller than local
accuracy demands, to keep $h \lambda_k$ inside its stability domain,
with $\{\lambda_k\}$ the eigenvalues of $J$ along the trajectory.
Stiffness thus depends on the spectrum of $J$, the integration horizon
and the tolerance. Chemical-kinetics networks with rate constants
spanning several orders of magnitude are stiff, as are many
discretised parabolic PDEs.

BDF/NDF and Rosenbrock4 have stability domains containing the left
half-plane or a wide wedge of it and suit stiff problems; Adams-Moulton
and Tsit5 do not, at any tolerance. The cost of a wrong choice is
asymmetric: an explicit method on a stiff problem fails or is forced
to uneconomic step sizes, an implicit method on a non-stiff problem
has a constant overhead per step. BDF/NDF is therefore the default
when the spectrum of $J$ is unknown; for a large model with a sparse
Jacobian it runs on the sparse linear solver (\texttt{sparse = TRUE}).

## Multistep methods

A linear multistep method determines $x_n$ from a linear combination
of the most recent $k+1$ states and right-hand-side values,
$\{x_{n-j}, f_{n-j}\}_{j=0}^{k}$. Reusing past steps, it reaches high
accuracy with few right-hand-side evaluations per step.

cppDE implements the BDF and Adams families in the Nordsieck
representation of SUNDIALS [@hindmarsh2005sundials]. Instead of the
past $k+1$ states it stores the \emph{scaled derivative array}
\[
  z_n =\left(x_n,\, h_n \dot{x}_n,\, \dfrac{h_n^2}{2!} \ddot{x}_n,
                  \,\dots,\,
                  \dfrac{h_n^{k}}{k!} x_n^{(k)} \right).
\]
A change of step size or order is then a linear transformation of
$z_n$, not a refit through past data.

### Backward Differentiation Formula ($\mathtt{bdf}$)

The BDF of order $q$ defines $x_n$ implicitly by
\begin{equation}
  \sum_{j=0}^{q} \alpha_j\, x_{n-j} \;=\; h_n\, f(x_n, t_n),
  \label{eq:bdf}
\end{equation}
which is exact whenever $x(t)$ is a polynomial of degree at most $q$
on the past $q+1$ nodes. It is A-stable for $q \le 2$ and
A($\alpha$)-stable for $q \in \{3,4,5\}$, with $\alpha$ falling
monotonically from $86^\circ$ at $q=3$ to $51^\circ$ at $q=5$.

The corrector \eqref{eq:bdf} is solved by Newton iteration,
\begin{equation}
  W \Delta x^{(\nu)} = - \tilde r \left(x_n^{(\nu)}\right),
  \qquad
  x_n^{(\nu+1)} = x_n^{(\nu)} + \Delta x^{(\nu)},
  \label{eq:newton}
\end{equation}
with leading coefficient $\beta_0 = 1/\alpha_0$ and iteration matrix
\begin{equation}
  W = \frac{1}{h_n\, \beta_0}\symbb{1} - J\bigl(x_n^{(\nu)}, t_n\bigr),
  \label{eq:bdf-W}
\end{equation}
in the SUNDIALS form [@hindmarsh2005sundials], which differs from the
textbook $I - h_n \beta_0\, J$ by the scalar factor $h_n \beta_0$.
Factorising $W$ dominates the cost of a step; the factorisation is
reused across steps.

cppDE defaults to the Numerical Differentiation Formula (NDF) variant
of Shampine and Reichelt [@MATLABODESuite], which adds to the BDF corrector a term proportional
to the Nordsieck predictor error,
\begin{equation}
\sum_{m=1}^{q} \dfrac{1}{m}\, \nabla^{m} x_n - h_n f(x_n, t_n) - \kappa_q\, \gamma_q\, \left(x_n - x_n^{\mathrm{pred}}\right) = 0, \qquad \gamma_q  = \sum_{m=1}^{q} \dfrac{1}{m}, \label{eq:ndf}
\end{equation}
with $\nabla$ the backward-difference operator. The term scales
$\beta_0$ in \eqref{eq:newton} by $(1 - \kappa_q)$ and multiplies the
leading truncation-error coefficient $1/(q+1)$ by
$1 + \kappa_q (q+1) \gamma_q$. With $\kappa_q < 0$ the truncation error
at fixed step size decreases, permitting a larger step at equal
accuracy. The values of $\kappa_q$ (Appendix \ref{app:bdf-coeffs})
give the step-size gains over classical BDF reported by
Shampine and Reichelt [@MATLABODESuite], $26\,\%$ for $q \le 3$ and $12\,\%$ for $q = 4$, at a
small loss of stability angle. \texttt{useNDF = FALSE} recovers
classical BDF ($\kappa_q \equiv 0$).

The corrector takes at most three iterations, each with one
right-hand-side evaluation and one linear solve. It has converged when
the damped correction norm $\delta\,\min(1, \rho)/\tau_q \le 1$, with
$\delta$ the WRMS norm of the latest correction, $\rho$ the estimated
contraction rate and $\tau_q$ an order-dependent constant. As in
CVODE, $W$ is refactorised when $\gamma = h_n\beta_0$ has moved by more
than $30\,\%$ since the last factorisation, after $20$ steps, or after
a failed corrector; $J$ is re-evaluated after $51$ steps or when a
failure is attributed to it. Without a new Jacobian, a sparse $W$
changes only on its diagonal.

### Adams-Moulton in PECE form ($\mathtt{adams}$)

The Adams-Moulton family integrates the interpolant of $f$ through
the $q+1$ samples $\{(t_{n-j}, f_{n-j})\}_{j=0}^{q}$ over $[t_{n-1}, t_n]$,
\begin{equation}
  x_n \;=\; x_{n-1} \;+\; h_n \sum_{j=0}^{q} \beta_j\,
            f(x_{n-j}, t_{n-j}),
  \label{eq:adams}
\end{equation}
implicit in $x_n$ through the $j=0$ term. cppDE solves it by
fixed-point iteration in predict-evaluate-correct-evaluate (PECE)
form, without Jacobian or linear solve: the Nordsieck predictor
supplies $x_n^{P}$, $f$ is evaluated there, and \eqref{eq:adams} is
applied with $f(x_n^{P}, t_n)$ in place of $f(x_n, t_n)$. Evaluation
and correction are repeated until convergence, at most three times in
all, as in CVODE. A step that converges on the first correction costs
two right-hand-side evaluations.

Its stability domain on the negative real axis shrinks rapidly with
order; for $q \ge 3$ it contains no wedge of $\mathbb{C}^-$, so the
method is unsuitable for stiff problems. For non-stiff problems with
smooth solutions and a long horizon, its maximum order
$q_{\max} = 12$ and two right-hand-side evaluations per step make it
competitive with fixed-order explicit Runge-Kutta methods.

## Single-step methods

Single-step methods carry no information beyond the current state and
reach order $p > 1$ through internal stages. They therefore restart
after an event at full order, whereas the multistep methods rebuild
the Nordsieck history from order $1$.

### Rosenbrock ($\mathtt{rb4}$)

A Rosenbrock method of $s$ stages with diagonal coefficient $\gamma$
linearises the implicit Runge-Kutta condition about $(x_n, t_n)$; its
stages $k_i$ solve
\begin{equation}
  W k_i = f\left(x_n + \sum_{j<i} \alpha_{ij}\, k_j,\,
                 t_n + c_i\, h_n \right) + \dfrac{1}{h_n} \sum_{j<i} \dfrac{\gamma_{ij}}{\gamma}\, k_j + h_n\, d_i\, \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial t}(x_n, t_n),
  \label{eq:rosenbrock-stage}
\end{equation}
with iteration matrix
\begin{equation}
  W = \frac{1}{\gamma\, h_n}\symbb{1} - J(x_n, t_n).
  \label{eq:rosenbrock-W}
\end{equation}
Table \ref{tab:rosenbrock-coeffs} lists the coefficients.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{@{}ll@{}}
\toprule
Symbol & Meaning \\
\midrule
$\alpha_{ij}$ & weights with which stage $i$ combines all earlier stages $k_j$, $j<i$ \\
$c_i$         & time abscissa of stage $i$ inside the step, with $c_i = \sum_{j<i}\alpha_{ij}$ \\
$\gamma_{ij}$ & weights with which the linear-solve correction at stage $i$ uses earlier stages \\
$\gamma$      & common diagonal coefficient appearing in the iteration matrix $W$ \\
$d_i$         & weights that pick up the explicit time dependence of $f$ via $\partial f/\partial t$ \\
$m_i$         & weights combining the stages into the advanced solution $x_{n+1}$ \\
$\hat{m}_i$   & weights combining the stages into the embedded order-3 estimator used for step control \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Rosenbrock method coefficients.}
\label{tab:rosenbrock-coeffs}
\end{table}

The advanced solution and embedded error estimate are
\[
  x_{n+1} = x_n + \sum_{i=1}^{s} m_i\, k_i,
  \qquad
  \hat{x}_{n+1} \;=\; x_n + \sum_{i=1}^{s} \hat{m}_i\, k_i.
\]
Each stage \eqref{eq:rosenbrock-stage} is one linear solve, without
Newton iteration. Per accepted step cppDE evaluates $J$ and factorises
$W$ once, evaluates the right-hand side five times and back-substitutes
six times.

cppDE uses the order-$4$ coefficients of Hairer and Wanner
[@hairer2010solving, §IV.7] (Appendix \ref{app:ros-coeffs}), the same set as the
\texttt{rosenbrock4} stepper of Boost.Numeric.Odeint: an L-stable pair
with an embedded order-$3$ estimator. Rosenbrock methods are competitive with BDF on
stiff problems whose Jacobian is cheap relative to the right-hand
side. With its full-order restart, Rosenbrock4 is the stiff method of
choice for systems with frequent state discontinuities at moderate
state dimension.

### Tsitouras ($\mathtt{tsit5}$)

Tsitouras is the explicit Runge-Kutta pair of order $5(4)$ derived by
Tsitouras [@TSITOURAS2011770] under the first column simplifying assumption alone,
\[
  \sum_{i=1}^{s} b_i\, a_{ij} \;=\; b_j\,(1 - c_j),
  \qquad j = 1, \dots, s,
\]
without the row simplifying assumption
$\sum_{j} a_{ij}\, c_j = c_i^2/2$, $i \ge 3$, on which the
Dormand-Prince pair rests. Tsitouras uses the freed parameters for a
smaller leading-error norm; the coefficients of Appendix
\ref{app:tsit5-coeffs} satisfy the column condition to rounding and
violate the row condition. The pair has $s = 7$ stages with the
First-Same-As-Last (FSAL) property,
\[
  k_7 \;=\; f(x_{n+1},\, t_n + h_n)
       \;=\; k_1 \text{ at step } n+1,
\]
so an accepted step costs six right-hand-side evaluations, not seven.
Table \ref{tab:tsit5-coeffs} defines the symbols.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{@{}ll@{}}
\toprule
Symbol & Meaning \\
\midrule
$a_{ij}$    & weights with which stage $i$ combines earlier stages (strictly lower triangular) \\
$c_i$       & time abscissa of stage $i$ inside the step, with $c_i = \sum_{j<i} a_{ij}$ \\
$b_i$       & weights combining the stages into the advanced order-5 solution; $b_7 = 0$ \\
$\hat{b}_i$ & weights combining the stages into the embedded order-4 estimator; $\hat{b}_7 \ne 0$ \\
$k_i$       & right-hand side at stage $i$: $k_i = f\!\left(x_n + h_n\sum_{j<i}a_{ij}k_j,\; t_n + c_i h_n\right)$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Symbols of the Tsit5 tableau.}
\label{tab:tsit5-coeffs}
\end{table}

The advanced solution and embedded error estimate are
\[
  x_{n+1} = x_n + h_n \sum_{i=1}^{7} b_i\, k_i,
  \qquad
  \hat{x}_{n+1} = x_n + h_n \sum_{i=1}^{7} \hat{b}_i\, k_i,
\]
and the local error estimate for step-size control is
\[
  e_{n+1} = h_n \sum_{i=1}^{7} (\hat{b}_i - b_i)\, k_i.
\]
Tsit5 needs neither Jacobian nor linear solve and, of the four
methods, advances furthest per right-hand-side evaluation. It suits
non-stiff problems with an expensive right-hand side.

## Adaptive step-size control

The error estimate $e_n$ of each method is reduced to a scalar by the
weighted root-mean-square norm
\begin{equation}
  \| e_n \|_{\mathrm{WRMS}} =
  \sqrt{\frac{1}{n_x} \sum_{j=1}^{n_x} \left(
    \frac{e_{n,j}}{w_{n,j}}
  \right)^{\!2}},
  \qquad
  w_{n,j} = \mathtt{atol} + \mathtt{rtol}\,|x^{\mathrm{ref}}_{n,j}|,
  \label{eq:wrms}
\end{equation}
whose weights put components of different magnitude and unit on a
common scale. The reference state $x^{\mathrm{ref}}_n$ is the accepted
solution $|x_n|$ at the start of the step in BDF/NDF and Adams, as in
CVODE, so the weights are fixed for the whole step, and the
component-wise maximum $\max(|x_n|, |x_{n+1}|)$ in the single-step
methods. A step is accepted when $\| e_n \|_{\mathrm{WRMS}} \le 1$.

The single-step methods choose the next step size with the
proportional-integral (PI) controller of Hairer and Wanner [@hairer2010solving]. With
$\varepsilon_n = \| e_n \|_{\mathrm{WRMS}}$ and $p$ the order of the
embedded estimate, $p = 3$ for Rosenbrock4 and $p = 4$ for Tsit5, an
accepted step sets
\[
  h_{n+1} = h_n\, \min\Bigl\{\rho_{\max},\; \max\Bigl(\rho_{\min},\;
        S\, \varepsilon_n^{-(\alpha+\beta)}\,
        \varepsilon_{n-1}^{\,\beta}\Bigr)\Bigr\},
  \qquad
  \alpha = \frac{0.7}{p+1}, \quad \beta = \frac{0.4}{p+1},
\]
with $S = 0.9$, $\rho_{\min} = 0.2$, $\rho_{\max} = 5$, and
$\varepsilon_{n-1}$ the norm of the previous accepted step, floored at
$0.01$. On the first step and after a rejection the integral factor
$S\,\varepsilon_n^{-1/(p+1)}$ replaces the PI factor, capped at $1$
after a rejection. A rejected step is retried with the factor
$S\,\varepsilon_n^{-1/(p+1)}$ clamped to $[\rho_{\min}, 0.9]$.

The multistep methods choose step size and order as CVODE does. With
$d_{q'}$ the WRMS norm of the error estimate at order $q'$, the
candidate ratios are
\[
  \eta_{q'} = \frac{1}{\bigl(B_{q'}\, d_{q'}\bigr)^{1/(q'+1)} + 10^{-6}},
  \qquad q' \in \{q-1,\, q,\, q+1\},
\]
with $B_{q-1} = B_q = 6$ and $B_{q+1} = 10$. The neighbouring orders
are compared $q+1$ steps after a change to order $q$ and every second
step while the order is unchanged; the largest ratio fixes the next
order. A ratio below $1.5$ leaves $h$ unchanged, and the ratio is
capped at $10^4$ on the first step and at $10$ afterwards.

### The first step

cppDE estimates the first step size from the initial state as in
Hairer, N\o{}rsett and Wanner [@hairer2008solving, Algorithm II.4.4]: a rough
$h_0 \sim \|x_0\| / \|f_0\|$ fixes a scale, a second derivative
$\ddot x$ along the trajectory fixes the curvature, and
\begin{equation}
  h_1 = \left(
    \frac{0.01}{\max\bigl(\|f_0\|, \|\ddot x\|\bigr)}
  \right)^{\!1/(p+1)}
  \label{eq:hnw-h1}
\end{equation}
turns the two into a step for a method of order $p$. The implicit
methods obtain $\ddot x = \partial f/\partial t + J f$ from the
generated Jacobian, the explicit one from a finite difference of $f$.
All norms are the weighted norms of \eqref{eq:wrms}; with
\texttt{sensErrCon = TRUE} they include the sensitivity components.

Two bounds apply, as in CVODE: an upper bound $h_{\mathrm{ub}}$,
capped by the remaining interval, keeps a single Euler step from
changing any component by more than a fraction of its own scale; a
lower bound $h_{\mathrm{lb}}$ keeps $h_0$ above the rounding of the
time variable. The multistep methods use a port of the CVODES routine
\texttt{cvHin}, which refines $\sqrt{h_{\mathrm{lb}} h_{\mathrm{ub}}}$
by a finite-difference curvature until two successive estimates agree
within a factor of two, so the first step equals the one CVODES takes
on the same problem. The estimator runs again after every event, on
the post-event state.

## Dense output

Requested output times in general do not coincide with the adaptive step grid.
Each accepted step therefore carries a local interpolant that yields
$x(t)$ anywhere inside the step by polynomial arithmetic alone,
without right-hand-side evaluations. With
$s = (t - t_n)/h_n \in [0, 1]$ the three families use:

- Tsit5: the cubic Hermite interpolant through $x_n$, $x_{n+1}$ and the
  FSAL derivatives $k_1$, $k_7$,
  \[
    x(t) = (1+2s)(1-s)^2\, x_n + s^2(3-2s)\, x_{n+1}
         + s(1-s)^2\, h_n k_1 + s^2(s-1)\, h_n k_7 .
  \]
- Rosenbrock4: the stage-based cubic of Hairer and Wanner [@hairer2010solving],
  \[
    x(t) = (1-s)\, x_n + s\bigl(x_{n+1} + (1-s)(c_3 + s\, c_4)\bigr),
    \qquad
    c_3 = \sum_{i=1}^{5} d_i^{(2)} k_i, \quad
    c_4 = \sum_{i=1}^{5} d_i^{(3)} k_i,
  \]
  with the coefficients of Table \ref{tab:ros-dense}.
- BDF/NDF and Adams: the Nordsieck polynomial of degree $q$ held after
  the step, $x(t) = \sum_{j=0}^{q} z_{n+1,j}\,
  \bigl((t - t_{n+1})/h_n\bigr)^{j}$.

Both single-step interpolants are of order $3$, below the order of the
step itself ($5$ for Tsit5, $4$ for Rosenbrock4); the multistep
interpolant has the order $q$ of the step.

## Forward sensitivities

### Dual-number arithmetic

Parameter sensitivities of the trajectory are computed by forward-mode
automatic differentiation [@griewank2008evaluating], not by finite
differences, whose truncation and round-off errors take several
integrations to control. Every floating-point scalar is augmented by a
component carrying its directional derivative. Arithmetic and
elementary functions are overloaded for the augmented type, so the C++
source that evaluates $f$ is compiled unchanged for the primal and the
sensitivity computation.

The augmented type is the \emph{dual number}
\[
  \tilde x = x + x'\,\varepsilon,
  \qquad \varepsilon^2 = 0,\quad \varepsilon \ne 0,
\]
with primal value $x \in \mathbb{R}$ and directional derivative
$x' \in \mathbb{R}$. Read as a first-order Taylor expansion in
$\varepsilon$, it obeys, for $\tilde x = x + x'\varepsilon$ and
$\tilde y = y + y'\varepsilon$,
\[
  \tilde x + \tilde y = (x+y) + (x'+y')\varepsilon,
  \qquad
  \tilde x \cdot \tilde y = xy + (xy' + x'y)\varepsilon,
\]
and for any smooth scalar function $g$,
\[
  g(\tilde x) = g(x) + g'(x)\,x'\,\varepsilon.
\]
Compositions carry the derivative of the composed function, so the
source that evaluates $f$ over $\mathbb{R}$ returns $f$ and its
directional derivative when called with dual inputs.

### Tangent storage

A dual stores its value inline and $m$ tangent slots behind a pointer;
$m$ is $\mathrm{ncol}$ of the tangent, set at run time rather than at
compile time. Tangents of temporaries come from a thread-local bump
arena, and everything a generated model body allocates there is
released in one operation when the body returns. State vectors the
stepper keeps across steps point into one contiguous $n_x \times m$
block per vector, the tangent slab, sized once per solve. A tangent
wider than one call should carry is split into blocks of directions;
since the step sequence of a tangent-blind solve does not depend on
$m$, the blocks share one grid and the assembled Hessian equals that of
a single pass exactly.

A dual whose width was never set has no slots and reads as a zero
tangent. Buffers zeroed before use, such as the cotangents of a
backward sweep, therefore get their width declared first; otherwise
their derivatives would be structurally zero.

### Sensitivity equations via dual evaluation

For a right-hand side depending on parameters
$p \in \mathbb{R}^{n_p}$,
\[
  \dot x = f(x, p, t), \qquad x(t_0) = x_0(p),
\]
the \emph{sensitivity matrix} is
\[
  S_p = \frac{\partial x}{\partial p} \in \mathbb{R}^{n_x \times n_p},
  \qquad
  (S_p)_{ij} = \frac{\partial x_i}{\partial p_j}.
\]
Seeding each state component with its row of $S_p$ gives the dual
state
\[
  \tilde x_i = x_i + (S_p)_{ij}\,\varepsilon_j,
\]
with dual unit $\varepsilon_j$ for direction $p_j$ and summation over
repeated indices. The $\varepsilon_j$-coefficient of the $i$-th output
of $f$ evaluated over the dual algebra is
\[
  \bigl[f(\tilde x, p, t)\bigr]_{i,\,\varepsilon_j}
  = \frac{\partial f_i}{\partial x_k}\,(S_p)_{kj}
    + \frac{\partial f_i}{\partial p_j}.
\]
The primal part recovers $\dot x_i = f_i(x,p,t)$; differentiating it
with respect to $p_j$ identifies the $\varepsilon_j$-coefficient with
$\dot{(S_p)}_{ij}$, which gives
\begin{equation}
  \dot S_p
    = \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\,S_p
      + \frac{\partial f}{\partial p},
  \qquad
  S_p(t_0) = \frac{\partial x_0}{\partial p}.
  \label{eq:sensitivity-p}
\end{equation}
One dual evaluation of $f$ thus yields the right-hand side of
\eqref{eq:sensitivity-p} for all columns of $S_p$, at a cost
proportional to $n_p$ and without forming $\partial f/\partial x$.

### Seeding: from $S_p$ to $S_\theta$

Inference parameters are often a vector $\theta \in \mathbb{R}^M$
linked to the dynamic parameters $p_{\mathrm{dyn}}$ and the initial
condition $x_0 = p_{\mathrm{init}}(\theta)$ by a reparametrisation
$p = \Phi(\theta)$. The quantity of interest is then
\[
  S_\theta = \frac{\partial x}{\partial \theta}
           \in \mathbb{R}^{n_x \times M},
\]
and the chain rule $S_\theta = S_p\,\partial p / \partial\theta$ turns
\eqref{eq:sensitivity-p} into
\begin{equation}
  \dot S_\theta
    = \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\,S_\theta
      + \frac{\partial f}{\partial p_{\mathrm{dyn}}}
        \,\frac{\partial p}{\partial \theta},
  \qquad
  S_\theta(t_0) = \frac{\partial p_{\mathrm{init}}}{\partial \theta}.
  \label{eq:sensitivity-theta}
\end{equation}
The matrix $\partial p / \partial\theta$, the \emph{tangent} of the
inputs, is passed as the \texttt{tangent} argument of
\texttt{solveODE()} and is fixed during integration. The choice
$\partial p/\partial\theta = I_{n_p}$ gives $S_\theta = S_p$; each of
the $M$ directions of $\theta$-space costs one additional state vector.

### Error norm with sensitivities

With forward sensitivities the integrator carries
$S_\theta \in \mathbb{R}^{n_x \times M}$ beside the state, and every
step produces $1+M$ error vectors of length $n_x$: $e_n^{(x)}$ for the
state and $e_S^{(k)}$ for each column $\partial x/\partial \theta_k$.
As in CVODES, they are combined by the maximum of the per-vector WRMS
norms, not by a flat WRMS over all $n_x(1+M)$ components.

The state norm $\| e_n^{(x)} \|_{\mathrm{WRMS}}$ is \eqref{eq:wrms}.
The column norm is its analogue with $S_\theta$ in place of $x$ in
error vector and weight,
\begin{equation}
  \| e_S^{(k)} \|_{\mathrm{WRMS}} =
  \sqrt{\frac{1}{n_x} \sum_{i=1}^{n_x} \left(
    \frac{(e_S)_{ik}}{w^{(k)}_{i}}
  \right)^{\!2}},
  \qquad
  w^{(k)}_{i} = \mathtt{atol} + \mathtt{rtol}\,|(S_\theta)_{ik}^{\mathrm{ref}}|,
  \label{eq:wrms-col}
\end{equation}
where $(S_\theta)_{ik}^{\mathrm{ref}}$ is taken like
$x^{\mathrm{ref}}_n$: the accepted value for multistep methods, the
maximum over both step ends for single-step methods. The step-size
controller uses the largest of these norms,
\begin{equation}
  \| e_n \|_{\mathrm{WRMS}} = \max\left\{
    \| e_n^{(x)} \|_{\mathrm{WRMS}},\;
    \max_{1 \le k \le M} \| e_S^{(k)} \|_{\mathrm{WRMS}}
  \right\}.
  \label{eq:wrms-sens}
\end{equation}
A flat WRMS divides by $n_x(1+M)$, so small errors in some columns can
mask a large error in another; the maximum holds each direction to the
requested tolerance separately.

The BDF/NDF corrector uses the same maximum, so an unconverged
sensitivity direction forces further iterations or a smaller step even
when the state has converged. With
\texttt{solveODE(..., sensErrCon = FALSE)}, error test, order
selection, corrector test and initial-step estimate use the state
components only, and the step sequence is that of a value run.

## Events and restarts

Two kinds of events interrupt smooth integration. A
*time-triggered event* fires at a time $t_e(\theta)$ given as a
closed-form expression, which may depend on $\theta$. A
*root-triggered event* fires when an event function $g_e(x, t)$
crosses zero along the trajectory, at the time $t^{*}(\theta)$ defined
implicitly by $g_e(x(t^{*}), t^{*}) = 0$. Either kind applies a
discontinuous reset
\[
  x^{+} = g(x^{-}, t),
\]
such as dosing a species, clipping to non-negative values, or
switching between dynamical regimes.

### Restart cost

Single-step methods (Rosenbrock4, Tsit5) resume after the reset with a
full-order step. Multistep methods (BDF/NDF, Adams) restart at order
$1$ and rebuild the Nordsieck array over several steps, which dominates
the cost on problems with frequent events. For every method the step
size is re-estimated from the post-event state by the initial-step
estimator of the solve, bounded by the remaining interval; for a
single-step method this is the whole restart.

### Sensitivity transport across a discontinuity

The reset $g$ acts on the trajectory $x(t, \theta)$ at the firing time
$t^{*}(\theta)$. The linearised update
$S_\theta^{+} = (\partial g/\partial x)\,S_\theta^{-}$ misses the
$\theta$-dependence of the firing time: a perturbation $\delta t^{*}$
adds short integrations of $\dot x = f$ on either side of the event,
with different right-hand sides before and after the reset. With
$f^{-}$ the right-hand side at $x^{-}$ and $f^{+}$ that at
$g(x^{-}, t^{*})$, the sensitivity at the first grid time after the
event receives two contributions beyond the linearised reset:

1. \emph{Pre-event drift.} $x^{-}$ flows along $\dot x = f^{-}$ from
   the grid time $t_*^{(0)} := \mathrm{scalar}(t^{*})$ to the perturbed
   firing time $t^{*}$, over $\delta t^{*} = t^{*} - t_*^{(0)}$, whose
   scalar part vanishes but whose $\theta$-derivatives do not.
2. \emph{Post-event drift.} The reset state $g(x^{-}, t^{*})$ flows
   along $\dot x = f^{+}$ from $t^{*}$ back to the grid time, over
   $-\delta t^{*}$.

Both contribute terms of order
$f^{\pm}\,(\partial t^{*}/\partial \theta)$; to first order they give
the saltation matrix of Section \ref{sec:saltation}.

cppDE replaces the bare reset by forward drift, reset and backward
drift, evaluated in dual arithmetic. Each drift is one step of Heun's
method, the explicit trapezoidal rule. Since $\delta t^{*}$ has scalar
part zero, the value of $x$ at the grid time is unchanged and only the
$\theta$-derivatives of the displacement enter the state. The reset
between the drifts is evaluated in the same arithmetic, so its first
and second derivatives enter as well. Without sensitivities, $g$ is
applied as a plain map.

The two kinds of event differ in how $\delta t$ is obtained: from the
expression $t_e(\theta)$, or by the implicit function theorem applied
to $g_e = 0$.

### Time-triggered events

For a firing time given as an expression $t_e(\theta)$, the
$\theta$-derivatives follow from the chain rule. The integrator runs
to the scalar grid time $t_e^{(0)} := \mathrm{scalar}(t_e)$ and treats
the displacement
\begin{equation}
  \delta t = t_e - t_e^{(0)},
  \qquad \mathrm{scalar}(\delta t) = 0,
  \label{eq:fixed-dt}
\end{equation}
as a dual number of value zero with first-order tangents
$\partial t_e/\partial \theta_a$ and second-order tangents
$\partial^2 t_e/\partial \theta_a \partial \theta_b$. The state at
$t_e^{(0)}$ is $x^{-}$; its first-order tangents are the pre-event
sensitivities $S_\theta$. The transport, a Heun step forward to $t_e$,
the reset, and a Heun step back to $t_e^{(0)}$ with the post-event
right-hand side, reads
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
  &\text{forward:}\quad
    f_1 = f(x^{-}, t_e^{(0)}), \quad
    x_E = x^{-} + f_1\,\delta t, \quad
    f_2 = f(x_E, t_e), \\
  &\hphantom{\text{forward:}\quad}
    x^{*} = x^{-} + \tfrac{1}{2}(f_1 + f_2)\,\delta t, \\
  &\text{reset:}\quad
    x^{*}_{+} = g(x^{*}, t_e), \\
  &\text{backward:}\quad
    \tilde f_1 = f(x^{*}_{+}, t_e), \quad
    x_B = x^{*}_{+} - \tilde f_1\,\delta t, \quad
    \tilde f_2 = f(x_B, t_e^{(0)}), \\
  &\hphantom{\text{backward:}\quad}
    x^{+} = x^{*}_{+} - \tfrac{1}{2}(\tilde f_1 + \tilde f_2)\,\delta t.
\end{aligned}
\label{eq:fixed-heun}
\end{equation}
An Euler step would suffice at first order: since
$\mathrm{scalar}(\delta t) = 0$, the powers $\delta t^{k}$, $k \ge 2$,
have no first-order dual content, so every $O(\delta t^{2})$ term drops
out of $\partial x^{+}/\partial \theta$. At second order the curvature
term
\[
  \tfrac{1}{2}\bigl(J\,f + \partial f/\partial t\bigr)\,\delta t^{2},
  \qquad J = \partial f/\partial x,
\]
keeps a second-order dual component, because $(\delta t)^{2}$, though
zero in value and first derivatives, has the mixed derivative
\[
  \frac{\partial^{2}(\delta t)^{2}}{\partial \theta_a\,\partial \theta_b}
    = 2\, \frac{\partial t_e}{\partial \theta_a}\,
          \frac{\partial t_e}{\partial \theta_b}.
\]
Heun's second evaluation, at the shifted state and the shifted time
$t_e$, supplies this term and leaves a truncation error of
$O(\delta t^{3})$. Evaluating $f_2$ and $\tilde f_2$ at $t_e^{(0)}$
instead would drop the $\tfrac{1}{2}(\partial f/\partial t)\,\delta t^{2}$
part for a right-hand side that depends explicitly on time.

### Root-triggered events

A root event fires at the time $t^{*}(\theta)$ defined implicitly by
\begin{equation}
  G(t^{*}(\theta), \theta) :=
    g_e\bigl(x(t^{*}(\theta), \theta), t^{*}(\theta)\bigr) = 0.
  \label{eq:root-condition}
\end{equation}
It is handled in three steps: localisation of $t^{*}$ on the scalar
trajectory, reconstruction of the dual residual $\delta t^{*}$ by the
implicit function theorem, and the Heun transport
\eqref{eq:fixed-heun}.

#### Localisation

The integrator evaluates $g_e$ at the end of every accepted step and at
every requested output time. A crossing on $[t_n, t_{n+1}]$ is accepted
when the two readings differ in sign, or when
$g_e(x_{n+1}, t_{n+1})$ is exactly zero, as for a root on a sampled
time. A zero at the lower end was reported with that sample and is not
a new crossing; this also keeps an event from firing again on the
surface it was just applied on, where $g_e$ is zero up to round-off.

The crossing is refined on the dense output of the accepted step,
without further right-hand-side evaluations, by false position with the
interpolation factor clamped to $[0.1, 0.9]$. The clamp bounds the
stagnation of the classical rule and keeps its speed on a nearly linear
$g_e$. The iteration stops when the bracket is narrower than the root
tolerance, after at most fifty iterations, or when an iterate gives
$g_e = 0$ exactly. It returns as $t_*^{(0)} := \mathrm{scalar}(t^{*})$
the end of the final bracket that still carries the pre-crossing sign
of $g_e$. Localisation yields no $\theta$-dependence of $t^{*}$, so the
dual residual $\delta t^{*} = t^{*} - t_*^{(0)}$ is reconstructed from
\eqref{eq:root-condition}.

#### Dual residual of the event time

If $G$ is smooth at the crossing and $\partial G/\partial t \neq 0$
there, the implicit function theorem applied to
\eqref{eq:root-condition} gives
\begin{equation}
  \frac{\partial t^{*}}{\partial \theta}
    = -\frac{G_\theta}{G_t}
    = -\frac{\nabla_x g_e \cdot S_\theta}
            {\nabla_x g_e \cdot f + \partial g_e/\partial t}\bigg|_{*},
  \label{eq:dt-star-first}
\end{equation}
whose denominator is the total time derivative
$\dot g_e = \nabla_x g_e \cdot f + \partial g_e/\partial t$ along the
trajectory at the crossing. The condition $\dot g_e \neq 0$ means a
transversal crossing of the event surface; at a grazing crossing the
firing time is not differentiable in $\theta$, and the fallback under
simultaneous events applies. In dual arithmetic
\eqref{eq:dt-star-first} is the quotient
\begin{equation}
  \delta t^{*} = -\frac{g_e(x^{-}, t_*^{(0)})}
                       {\dot g_e(x^{-}, t_*^{(0)})},
  \label{eq:dt-star-quotient}
\end{equation}
with $g_e$ and $\dot g_e$ evaluated on the dual state $x^{-}$ at the
scalar grid time. The generated partials $\nabla_x g_e$ and
$\partial g_e/\partial t$ are needed only for $\dot g_e$; the dual
arithmetic forms $\nabla_x g_e \cdot S_\theta$ in the numerator. The
scalar value of the numerator, of the order of the root tolerance, is
set to zero before the division, so $\delta t^{*}$ is zero in value and
carries only derivatives.

The first-order part of \eqref{eq:dt-star-quotient} equals
\eqref{eq:dt-star-first}. At second order the quotient lacks the
$G_{tt}$ contribution, because $g_e$ is evaluated at the scalar time
$t_*^{(0)}$, not at the dual time $t^{*}$. Expanding
\eqref{eq:root-condition} to second order in $\theta$ with
$\delta t^{*} = \delta t^{*}_{(1)} + \delta t^{*}_{(2)} + \cdots$ and
$G(t_*^{(0)}, \theta^{(0)}) = 0$ gives
\[
  0 = G_t\,\delta t^{*}_{(2)}
      + \tfrac{1}{2} G_{tt}\,(\delta t^{*}_{(1)})^{2}
      + G_{t\theta}\,\delta t^{*}_{(1)}\,\delta\theta
      + \tfrac{1}{2} G_{\theta\theta}\,\delta\theta^{2},
\]
of which the quotient supplies the $G_{t\theta}$ and
$G_{\theta\theta}$ terms. The corrected update is
\begin{equation}
  \delta t^{*} \leftarrow \delta t^{*}
    - \tfrac{1}{2}\,\frac{G_{tt}}{G_t}\,(\delta t^{*})^{2},
  \label{eq:dt-star-second}
\end{equation}
where
\[
  G_{tt} = \frac{\mathrm{d}^{2}}{\mathrm{d} t^{2}}
            g_e\bigl(x(t), t\bigr)\bigg|_{*}
\]
is the second total time derivative of $g_e$ along the trajectory,
taken from generated code or, where that is not available, from a
forward finite difference of $\dot g_e$. The correction
\eqref{eq:dt-star-second} changes only the second-order components of
$\delta t^{*}$.

The Heun transport \eqref{eq:fixed-heun} then carries $x^{-}$ across
the event to the grid time $t_*^{(0)}$, with $\delta t^{*}$ in place of
$\delta t$ and $t_*^{(0)} + \delta t^{*}$ in place of $t_e$.

#### Simultaneous events

Several root conditions can cross zero within one accepted step. Each
crossing is localised separately, and those that share $t_*^{(0)}$
within the localisation tolerance form a cluster. For a cluster, one
forward Heun shift reaches the common event surface, every triggered
reset is applied there (the reset maps are assumed to commute), and
one backward shift returns to the grid time: four right-hand-side
evaluations regardless of the number of events. The dual residual
$\delta t^{*}$ is computed once, from the first event in the cluster
with non-zero $\dot g_e$, and shared by the others, which sit at the
same grid time with the same parameter dependence through $x^{-}$.

If every event in the cluster has $\dot g_e = 0$ at the surface, the
denominator of \eqref{eq:dt-star-first} vanishes and the implicit
function theorem gives no $\partial t^{*}/\partial \theta$. cppDE
detects this case by the size of $|\dot g_e|$ and applies the reset as
a plain map without transport, which is exact in the limit where both
contributions $f^{\pm}\,(\partial t^{*}/\partial \theta)$ vanish.

#### Conditions switched by a reset

A root condition that a reset makes true escapes the sign-change
search, since a jump is not a crossing of the continuous solution.
Every condition is therefore evaluated on both sides of a jump. A
condition whose sign changes across the jump fires there, one per
sweep so that a reset can switch on the next condition; one that
already held before the jump does not fire again.

The switched resets are applied at the jump, between the forward and
the backward shift of the event that caused it, not after the
transport has returned to the grid time. One Heun transport then
carries the composition of both resets, and its first- and
second-order sensitivities equal those of the same reset written as a
time-triggered event at that time.

Terminal conditions are excluded: they stop the integration instead of
resetting the state.

### Connection to the saltation matrix \label{sec:saltation}

The classical \emph{saltation matrix} adds to the reset Jacobian
$\partial g/\partial x$ a term for the $\theta$-dependence of the
firing time:
\[
  S_\theta^{+} = \frac{\partial g}{\partial x}\,S_\theta^{-}
    + \left( \frac{\partial g}{\partial t}
             + \frac{\partial g}{\partial x}\,f^{-} - f^{+} \right)
       \frac{\partial t^{*}}{\partial \theta}.
\]
The first-order part of the Heun transport equals this expression,
with $\partial t^{*}/\partial \theta = \partial t_e/\partial \theta$
for time-triggered events and $\partial t^{*}/\partial \theta$ from
\eqref{eq:dt-star-first} for root events. The transport also yields
the second-order sensitivities, which the saltation matrix does not.
It is implemented in \texttt{cppde\_saltation.hpp}, the event loop in
\texttt{cppde\_event\_engine.hpp}.

## Reverse-mode sensitivities: the discrete adjoint \label{sec:reverse}

Forward sensitivities cost one additional state vector per direction
in $\theta$, so the gradient of a scalar objective over $M$ parameters
costs $M$ times the value alone. For a single scalar $J$, such as a
likelihood or a residual sum of squares, the transposed computation
delivers the whole gradient at a cost independent of $M$
[@griewank2008evaluating; @naumann2012art]. cppDE builds this mode with
\verb|cppODE(..., derivMode = "reverse")|.

The reverse mode computes a contraction, not the sensitivity matrix.
Given a cotangent $W \in \mathbb{R}^{n_t \times n_x}$ on the observed
trajectory, one sweep returns
\begin{equation}
  \bar\theta_j
    = \sum_{o=1}^{n_t} \sum_{i=1}^{n_x}
      W_{oi} \,
      \frac{\partial x_i(t_o)}{\partial \theta_j},
  \qquad j = 1,\dots,n_x+n_p,
  \label{eq:adjoint-contraction}
\end{equation}
where $o$ runs over the observation times and $i$ over the state
components. Row $o$ of $W$ is written $w_o \in \mathbb{R}^{n_x}$, the
cotangent at $t_o$. For a least-squares objective $W$ is the residual
weighted by the error model, and $\bar\theta$ is $\nabla_\theta J$
exactly. Several cotangents may be supplied as columns of a
three-dimensional array, one sweep each.

### The adjoint equation

The contraction \eqref{eq:adjoint-contraction} can be evaluated
without forming $S_p$, the forward sensitivity of
\eqref{eq:sensitivity-p}. Both backends implement the classical
construction below, with different discretisations. Define
$\lambda(t) \in \mathbb{R}^{n_x}$ backwards from the end of the
observed interval by
\begin{equation}
  \dot\lambda = -J(x, p, t)^{\mathsf T}\lambda,
  \qquad \lambda(T^+) = 0,
  \qquad \lambda(t_o^-) = \lambda(t_o^+) + w_o,
  \label{eq:adjoint-ode}
\end{equation}
so that $\lambda$ is continuous between observation times and jumps by
the cotangent row at each. Along the solution the two Jacobian terms
cancel,
\begin{equation}
  \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}
    \left(\lambda^{\mathsf T} S_p\right)
    = -\lambda^{\mathsf T} J S_p
      + \lambda^{\mathsf T}\!
        \left(J S_p + \frac{\partial f}{\partial p}\right)
    = \lambda^{\mathsf T} \frac{\partial f}{\partial p},
  \label{eq:adjoint-identity}
\end{equation}
so $\lambda$ is defined without reference to $\theta$. Integrating
\eqref{eq:adjoint-identity} over $[t_0, T]$ and collecting the jumps,
which contribute exactly the terms of \eqref{eq:adjoint-contraction},
gives
\begin{equation}
  \bar\theta
    = \left(\frac{\partial x_0}{\partial \theta}\right)^{\!\mathsf T}\!
      \lambda(t_0)
    + \left(\frac{\partial p}{\partial \theta}\right)^{\!\mathsf T}\!
      \int_{t_0}^{T}
      \left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial p}\right)^{\!\mathsf T}\!\lambda(t)\,
      \mathrm{d}t .
  \label{eq:adjoint-result}
\end{equation}
When $\theta$ consists of the initial state and the parameters
themselves, both outer factors are identities and a reverse solve
reports the pair
\begin{equation}
  \bar x_0 = \lambda(t_0),
  \qquad
  \bar p = \int_{t_0}^{T}
    \left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial p}\right)^{\!\mathsf T}\!\lambda(t)\,
    \mathrm{d}t.
  \label{eq:adjoint-quadrature}
\end{equation}
A reparametrisation $p = \Phi(\theta)$ is applied afterwards through
the outer factors of \eqref{eq:adjoint-result}, the chain rule of
\eqref{eq:sensitivity-theta} applied on the left.

The gradient costs one backward solve of a linear system of dimension
$n_x$ and a quadrature of dimension $n_p$, whatever $M$;
$\partial f/\partial p$ enters only contracted with $\lambda$ and is
never formed. The two parts of \eqref{eq:adjoint-quadrature} are
returned stacked in the row order of the \texttt{tangent} argument,
states first, then parameters.

### Discrete and continuous adjoints

Equation \eqref{eq:adjoint-ode} describes the exact trajectory; cppDE
provides both common discretisations of it. The \emph{continuous}
adjoint differentiates, then discretises: \eqref{eq:adjoint-ode} is
solved backwards by an integrator of its own over forward states
recovered by interpolation [@cao2003adjoint]. This is the route of
CVODES, exposed by \texttt{cvode()} (Section \ref{sec:asa}). The
\emph{discrete} adjoint, implemented by \texttt{cppODE()}, reverses
that order: it transposes the map the forward run applied, one
accepted step at a time. Both approximate the same gradient and
converge as the tolerance is lowered. They differ in three respects.

\textbf{Consistency of value and gradient.} The discrete adjoint
differentiates the computed trajectory and returns the derivative of
the reported value, up to rounding. The continuous adjoint approximates
the derivative of the exact solution, which no run computes, so its
gradient is consistent with the accompanying value only to
$O(\mathrm{tol})$, and tightening the backward tolerance alone does not
remove the difference.

\textbf{Discontinuities.} A jump in the state implies a jump in
$\lambda$, given by the transposed saltation matrix of the event. The
continuous adjoint restarts its backward integration with that matrix
at every event; in the discrete adjoint the jump is the transpose of
arithmetic the forward run performed, handled like any other step.

\textbf{Linear algebra per step.} The discrete adjoint of an implicit
step is one transposed solve against the step's iteration matrix,
evaluated at the checkpointed state, with neither Newton iteration nor
error control. The continuous adjoint integrates a stiff linear ODE
with its own step-size control and step count.

### The step map and its adjoint

Reverse accumulation has no counterpart in an augmented arithmetic: a
dual number carries its derivative with its value, available as soon
as an operation has executed, whereas an adjoint sums over all later
uses of a quantity. A step's adjoint is obtained either by recording
its operations on a tape and traversing it backwards, or in closed
form, since the map is one accepted step of a known method on a fixed
grid. cppDE uses the closed form and keeps no tape.

An accepted step of the multistep family decomposes into the Nordsieck
rescale and Pascal shift, the corrector, and the tail the controller
applies between the acceptance of this step and the next:
\begin{align}
  z^{\text{pred}} &= A\, z^{\text{in}}, \label{eq:step-pred}\\
  r(y, z^{\text{pred}}, \theta) &= 0, \label{eq:step-corr}\\
  z^{\text{out}} &= B\, z^{\text{pred}} + c\, a, \qquad a = y - z^{\text{pred}}_0.
  \label{eq:step-tail}
\end{align}
The operators $A$, $B$ and $c$ act on the slot index only; their
coefficients follow from the carry and are the same for every state
component. They are read off the stepper, not transposed by hand: a
probe whose states are the Nordsieck slots is driven through the
routines of the forward step, carrying the identity in the
$[\text{slot} \times \text{component}]$ array, and one pass returns
every column. The adjoint therefore uses exactly the coefficients of
the forward step.

The corrector is differentiated by the implicit function theorem.
Since $\partial r/\partial y$ is the iteration matrix
$W = I - \gamma J$ the forward step factorises, one transposed solve
against $W$ replaces the Newton iteration. For the Rosenbrock family
the counterpart is a transposed stage recursion, six solves against one
factorisation; for an explicit method, the backward recursion over the
tableau.

The code generator emits the contractions the adjoint requires beside
the right-hand side: $J^{\mathsf T}\lambda$,
$(\partial f/\partial p)^{\mathsf T}\lambda$ and, for a Rosenbrock
method, the same two applied to $J v$, which carry a second derivative
because the stages solve against a matrix built from the Jacobian.

### Checkpoint per step

The forward run stores one checkpoint per accepted step: the
step-start state, the carry, the time, the step size, and a record of
the operations the controller applied to the carry afterwards. Memory
is linear in the number of steps and holds no derivatives. The
factorisations of the forward run are not kept, so the sweep re-forms
and refactorises the iteration matrix at each checkpoint. The slot
operators are cached, keyed on the carry and the step size, so the
probe runs only where the controller changed the control state.

Observations lie at interpolated times and are evaluated through the
continuous extension of the step containing them. The adjoint of that
evaluation comes from the same probe: after the tail, the probe holds
a valid interpolant, and evaluating it at the observation time yields
the row $\partial x_{\text{interp}} / \partial (z^{\text{pred}}, a)$
directly.

### Checkpoint reuse

The sweep reads only the checkpoints, so the forward and backward
passes can be separate calls. A reverse solve with
\texttt{keepStore = TRUE} returns its checkpoints as \verb|$store|; a
later solve of the same model at the same times and parameters accepts
them through \texttt{store}, performs no integration and proceeds
directly to the sweep. A store created at a different parameter value
is rejected. The call that creates a store may omit the cotangent and
then performs a value-only run.

A gradient needs two solves at the same parameter value, one for the
values from which the cotangent is formed and one for the sweep; the
store removes the second integration. The columns of a
three-dimensional cotangent sweep the one store in turn, so
$n_{\text{seed}}$ cotangents cost $n_{\text{seed}}$ sweeps and a single
integration.

Under \verb|derivMode = "forward-reverse"| both arguments are refused:
a checkpoint of that mode carries tangents, which live in the arena of
the recording solve and do not outlive it, so every second-order sweep
is preceded by its own integration.

### The adjoint of an event

An event is a map of its own between two steps. The forward run
transports the discontinuity with the Heun sandwich of Section
\ref{sec:saltation}: a shift to the event surface, the resets, and a
shift back to the grid time. Each shift is taken over the residual of
the event time, which is zero in value and carries only derivatives.
In value the jump is therefore a plain jump, and the sandwich reduces
to the classical saltation relation
\begin{equation}
  \mathrm{d}x = R'\!\left(\mathrm{d}x_{\text{before}} + f_{\text{before}}\, s\right)
              - f_{\text{after}}\, s,
  \label{eq:saltation}
\end{equation}
with $R$ the resets, $R'$ their Jacobian and $s$ the differential of the
event time. For a root event $g(x, t, p) = 0$ the implicit function
theorem gives
$s = -(\nabla g \cdot \mathrm{d}x + \partial g/\partial p \cdot
\mathrm{d}p) / \dot g$; for a fixed event at $t = \tau(p)$,
$s = (\partial \tau/\partial p)\cdot \mathrm{d}p$.

Equation \eqref{eq:saltation} is linear in $\mathrm{d}x_{\text{before}}$
and $\mathrm{d}p$, so its transpose can be read off. Contracting it
with a cotangent $\lambda_{\text{after}}$ and collecting the terms that
multiply $s$ leaves one scalar $\kappa$,
\begin{equation}
  \kappa = \lambda_{\text{after}}^{\mathsf T}
           \left(R' f_{\text{before}} - f_{\text{after}}\right),
  \qquad
  \lambda_{\text{before}}
    = R'^{\mathsf T}\lambda_{\text{after}}
    + \kappa \left(\frac{\partial s}{\partial x}\right)^{\!\mathsf T},
  \label{eq:saltation-adjoint}
\end{equation}
and the parameter cotangent additionally receives
$\kappa\,(\partial s/\partial p)^{\mathsf T}$. For a root event both
derivatives of $s$ carry the factor $-\kappa/\dot g$: the state picks up
$-(\kappa/\dot g)\nabla g$ and the parameters
$-(\kappa/\dot g)\,\partial g/\partial p$. For a fixed event
$\partial s/\partial x = 0$ and the parameters pick up
$\kappa\,\partial\tau/\partial p$.

The transpose $R'^{\mathsf T}$ is applied reset by reset, in reverse
order. A reset that replaces a state removes the incoming cotangent of
that component, one that adds to it leaves the cotangent unchanged, and
one that multiplies it by $h$ scales it by $h$; where $h$ depends on
the state or the parameters, its derivatives enter the same transpose.
The adjoint of a jump therefore requires the right-hand side at both
ends, $\nabla g$ and $\dot g$, and the model's derivatives of the reset
and event-time expressions, but no Jacobian of $f$: every term the two
shifts would contribute carries the residual as a factor, and that
factor is zero.

After a jump the multistepper restarts: \verb|initialize| builds the
Nordsieck history from a single state as $z_0 = x$ and
$z_1 = h\, f(x, t)$, with the remaining slots zero, so the cotangent of
the history collapses onto that state. With $w_j$ the cotangent of
slot $j$, the restart contributes
\begin{equation}
  \bar x = w_0 + h\, J^{\mathsf T} w_1,
  \qquad
  \bar p = h \left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial p}\right)^{\!\mathsf T} w_1,
  \label{eq:restart-collapse}
\end{equation}
and slots above the first contribute nothing. The same map applies at
the start of the trajectory.

### Second order of an event's adjoint

The differential $s$ of the event time is zero in value, with
$\mathrm{d}s \neq 0$, so
\begin{equation}
  s^{2} = 0, \qquad \mathrm{d}\!\left(s^{2}\right) = 2 s\,\mathrm{d}s = 0,
  \qquad \mathrm{d}^{2}\!\left(s^{2}\right) = 2\,(\mathrm{d}s)^{2} \neq 0 ,
  \label{eq:s-squared}
\end{equation}
and terms of order $s^{2}$ drop from the gradient but not from the
Hessian. Three such terms enter a jump. The same three enter a fixed
event, with the event time's own residual
$\tau = \varepsilon(\theta) - \lfloor \varepsilon \rceil$ in place of
$s$: a fixed event is the same five-stage sandwich
\eqref{eq:root-sandwich}, and its transpose is that program reversed
with $\tau$ substituted throughout. The classical saltation alone is
exact in value but wrong in the tangents once the jump height moves
with a parameter, because
$\bar x_{a} = (I - \tau J_{a})^{\mathsf T}\bar x_{o}$ then has a second
factor that is not zero in value.

The first term is the curvature of the shift. Each half of the
sandwich is a Heun step,
\begin{equation}
  x_{\ast} = x_{\text{before}} + f_{\text{before}}\, s
           + \tfrac{1}{2}\, a_{\text{before}}\, s^{2},
  \qquad
  a = \frac{\partial f}{\partial x} f + \frac{\partial f}{\partial t},
  \label{eq:heun-curvature}
\end{equation}
and $a\,s$ is the difference of the two right-hand sides the step
already evaluates, so no Jacobian is needed.

The second is the post-jump state, which the sweep reconstructs
because the store keeps only $x_{\text{before}}$. Rebuilt from the bare
reset it would satisfy $\partial x_{\text{after}} / \partial t^{*} = 0$,
whereas
\begin{equation}
  \frac{\partial x_{\text{after}}}{\partial t^{*}}
    = f_{\text{before}} - f_{\text{after}} ,
  \label{eq:post-jump-motion}
\end{equation}
so the reconstruction runs the sandwich, not the reset.

The third comes from the quadrature. The parameter cotangent
\begin{equation}
  \bar p_{k} = \int_{0}^{T} G_{k}\,\mathrm{d}t
             = \int_{0}^{t^{*}} + \int_{t^{*}}^{T},
  \qquad
  G_{k} = \left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial p_{k}}\right)^{\!\mathsf T}\!\lambda,
  \label{eq:quadrature-split}
\end{equation}
is split at $t^{*}$, where $G_{k}$ jumps with the state.
Differentiating a split integral with a moving split point leaves the
jump of the integrand at the split,
\begin{equation}
  \frac{\partial \bar p_{k}}{\partial v}
  \;\supset\;
  \Big( G_{k}(t^{*-}) - G_{k}(t^{*+}) \Big)\,
  \frac{\partial t^{*}}{\partial v} .
  \label{eq:quadrature-jump}
\end{equation}
Only parameters whose $\partial f / \partial p_{k}$ depends on a state
the reset changed contribute.

Implemented as accumulations scaled by the residual, all three are
zero in value and carry $\partial t^{*} / \partial v$ in their tangent,
so the gradient is unchanged. For a fixed event at $t = \tau(p)$ the
residual is $\tau - \lfloor \tau \rceil$; for a root event it is
\begin{equation}
  s = -\,\frac{g - \lfloor g \rceil}{\dot g},
  \qquad
  \dot g = \frac{\partial g}{\partial t} + \nabla g \cdot f ,
  \label{eq:root-residual}
\end{equation}
read at the stored state. Localisation ignores the tangents, so that
state carries $\partial x / \partial \theta$ at a fixed time and
$\nabla g$ contracts it to the event time's.

### Transposing the root sandwich

The jump is the composition
\begin{equation}
  x_{e} = x_{b} + f_{b} s, \quad
  x_{\ast} = x_{b} + \tfrac{1}{2}(f_{b} + f_{e}) s, \quad
  x_{a} = R(x_{\ast}), \quad
  x_{k} = x_{a} - f_{a} s, \quad
  x_{o} = x_{a} - \tfrac{1}{2}(f_{a} + f_{k}) s ,
  \label{eq:root-sandwich}
\end{equation}
with $f_{e} = f(x_{e}, t^{*})$, $f_{a} = f(x_{a}, t^{*})$ and
$f_{k} = f(x_{k}, t_{0})$. This straight-line program is transposed
assignment by assignment, not through a collected closed form: a
collected form pruned by order in $s$, keeping a product only where one
factor does not vanish in value, is valid for the gradient but, by
\eqref{eq:s-squared}, not for the Hessian.

Reversed this way, the shift receives a contribution from every
assignment in which it occurs, including two from evaluating $f_{e}$
and $f_{a}$ at $t^{*}$, which depends on $\theta$:
\begin{equation}
  \bar s \;\supset\;
    \left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}\right)_{\!(x_{a}, t^{*})}\!\!\cdot \bar f_{a}
    + \left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}\right)_{\!(x_{e}, t^{*})}\!\!\cdot \bar f_{e} .
  \label{eq:shift-clock}
\end{equation}
Both cotangents carry a factor $s$, so \eqref{eq:shift-clock} is absent
from the gradient and enters the Hessian at full strength. It vanishes
identically for an autonomous right-hand side; a pruned form omits it
whenever $\partial f/\partial t \neq 0$.

The forward path corrects the shift by
$-\tfrac{1}{2}(\ddot g / \dot g)\,s^{2}$, whose chain factor
$1 + 2 c_{2} s$, $c_{2} = -\ddot g / (2\dot g)$, is one in value and a
second-order tangent; the transpose carries it on
$\partial s / \partial x$.

The sweep binds the tangent storage of every buffer it hands to a
generated contraction (Section \ref{sec:fwdrev}). In the jump transpose
every read of such a buffer is multiplied by $s$, so an unbound buffer
would leave value and gradient intact and make the Hessian wrong by a
rank-one term.

\textbf{Derivative of the shift.} Since $\dot g$ depends on the state,
\begin{equation}
  \frac{\partial s}{\partial x}
    = -\frac{\nabla g}{\dot g} - \frac{s}{\dot g}\, \nabla \dot g ,
  \qquad
  \nabla \dot g = \nabla \frac{\partial g}{\partial t}
                + \left(\nabla^{2} g\right) f + J^{\mathsf T}\nabla g ,
  \label{eq:root-quotient}
\end{equation}
and the second term carries $g$, which is zero in value: absent from
the gradient, full strength in the Hessian. A $g$ linear in the state
and independent of time reduces $\nabla \dot g$ to
$J^{\mathsf T}\nabla g$ and leaves the other two terms untested, so the
generator differentiates
$\dot g = \partial g/\partial t + \nabla g \cdot f$ as one expression
rather than assembling three terms. This yields
$\nabla \partial g/\partial t$ and $(\nabla^{2} g) f$ and, on $\theta$,
the matching $\partial^{2} g/\partial\theta\,\partial t$,
$(\partial \nabla g/\partial\theta)\cdot f$ and
$(\partial f/\partial\theta)^{\mathsf T}\nabla g$. A forcing inside $g$
is differentiated in $t$ through its rate: the time derivative on the
expression graph seeds each forcing leaf with a rate leaf, which prints
as the derivative of the PCHIP interpolant.

\textbf{Time-dependent resets.} A reset value $h$ that depends
explicitly on time is applied on the surface, at $t^{*}$, so
\begin{equation}
  \frac{\partial x_{a}}{\partial t^{*}} \;\supset\; c\,
  \frac{\partial h}{\partial t}, \qquad
  c = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{add} \\ 1 & \text{replace} \\ x_{\ast k} &
  \text{multiply,}\end{cases}
  \label{eq:reset-clock}
\end{equation}
which contributes to $\kappa$ of \eqref{eq:saltation-adjoint}. This
term is first order: omitting it makes the gradient wrong, not only the
Hessian. For the same reason the transposed reset receives the event
time as a dual rather than a plain number, so that
$\partial h/\partial\theta$ carries the dependence of $t^{*}$ on
$\theta$. Such a value evaluates $t^{*}$ directly and inherits the root
tolerance rather than the integration tolerance; in a value that
depends only on the state at $t^{*}$ the localisation error is damped
by the smoothness of the trajectory.

\textbf{Verification.} With $R = \mathrm{id}$ the composition
\eqref{eq:root-sandwich} is the identity and the transpose cancels term
by term. Against a nested-dual evaluation of the same sandwich, without
solver, store or event engine, the transpose is exact to
$9\cdot10^{-16}$. Over a whole trajectory, compared with forward over
forward on one recorded step sequence, the second order agrees to the
tolerance of the solve. Only this last check is sensitive to
\eqref{eq:shift-clock}: the nested-dual check compares against the same
forward routine the transpose reverses, so a term absent from both
sides cancels.

### Verifying a derivative across a moving event

When $t^{*}$ depends on a parameter, the reported trajectory carries a
row whose time moves with it. A functional $w^{\mathsf T} x$ seeded on
that row differs between parameter values and has no derivative to
compare against. Restricting the cotangent to the user's own output
times restores a well-posed functional, and the forward,
forward-over-forward and difference-quotient answers then agree to the
tolerance of the solve.

### Internal numerical differentiation

The step sizes the controller selected are constants of the
differentiated map. This is Bock's internal numerical differentiation:
the nominal run adapts freely, and the derivative is taken of the
scheme that run applied. Differentiating the control law instead adds
derivatives of the step sizes to the chain rule and makes the discrete
adjoint inconsistent with the adjoint ODE; that term, measured at
$O(\text{tol})$, is left out.

The usual justification, that $h$ is piecewise constant in $\theta$
with zero derivative almost everywhere, does not hold for an adaptive
controller, and the argument below does not rely on it. Let
$y_{h}(\theta)$ be the result the program returns on the grid the
controller selects at $\theta$. Then
\begin{equation}
  \frac{\mathrm{d} y_{h}}{\mathrm{d}\theta}
    = \frac{\partial y_{h}}{\partial \theta}
    + \sum_{k} \frac{\partial y_{h}}{\partial h_{k}}\,
      \frac{\mathrm{d} h_{k}}{\mathrm{d}\theta} ,
  \label{eq:grid-effect}
\end{equation}
where internal numerical differentiation computes the first term and
the sum is the grid effect, which differentiating the control law would
add.

The step size $h(\theta)$ is piecewise smooth with jumps: within an
acceptance region it varies smoothly through the error estimate, and at
its boundary an accepted step is rejected and the entire later grid
shifts. Halving the spacing of a sweep in $\theta$ doubles the measured
magnitude of the grid effect, which identifies it as a jump height
divided by $\Delta\theta$, not a derivative. Automatic differentiation
reproduces only the smooth part, so differentiating the control law
returns the exact gradient plus the smooth part of the grid effect,
without the jump part, which is the larger of the two. The result is
neither the derivative of the exact solution, to which the addition
does not belong, nor that of the reported value, whose dominant
contribution is missing. Recovering the grid effect requires a smoothed
controller, a fixed grid or a randomised estimator, none of which
differentiating the existing chain provides.

By this criterion the forward mode departs from internal numerical
differentiation and the reverse does not. The value pass of the reverse
mode runs the stepper on plain numbers, so the step sizes follow from
the state error alone and the derivative is taken on the grid of the
nominal run. The forward mode with the default
\texttt{sensErrCon = TRUE} maximises its error norm over the
sensitivity columns as in \eqref{eq:wrms-sens} and integrates on a
finer grid, to which no reported value belongs. The reverse gradient is
thus the derivative of the trajectory a value run returns, the forward
gradient that of a trajectory that is not reported, and the
$O(\mathrm{tol})$ difference between them is mainly due to the forward
mode.

The default keeps the sensitivities in the error norm because they are
integrated alongside the state and their errors accumulate; CVODES
guards against this in the same way (\texttt{CVodeSetSensErrCon}).
Value and gradient on slightly different grids is the smaller cost.
\texttt{solveODE(..., sensErrCon = FALSE)} selects the alternative.

### Goal-oriented step-size control

A grid selected from the state error alone need not be fine enough for
the gradient: a step at which $\lambda$ is large contributes strongly to
the error in $J$ even where its own state error is small, so the
gradient inherits the order of the state error but not its constant.
The forward mode settles this within the run by maximising the error
norm over the sensitivity columns as in \eqref{eq:wrms-sens}. The
reverse mode cannot, because $\lambda$ at step $k$ depends on every
later step and is not available while step $k$ is taken.

It is available across runs. The \texttt{errWeights} argument of
\texttt{solveODE()} takes the $\lambda$ of an earlier sweep, sampled on
that sweep's grid, interpolates it linearly and enters it into the
error norm as
\begin{equation}
  \mathrm{err} = \max\!\left(
    \mathrm{err}_{\text{state}},\;
    \frac{\left|\lambda(t_{n+1})^{\mathsf T} e_n\right|}{\mathtt{gradtol}}
  \right),
  \label{eq:goal-oriented}
\end{equation}
where $e_n$ is the embedded error estimate of the step. The numerator
estimates the step's contribution to the error in the objective, and
\texttt{gradtol}, the tolerance to which that contribution is held,
makes the two terms comparable.

Because of the maximum, the grid can only become finer than
\texttt{abstol} and \texttt{reltol} require, never coarser, and the
accuracy of the trajectory is unaffected. An inaccurate $\lambda$ costs
at most computing time: too large, and the steps are unnecessarily
small; too small, and the state term governs as before. An estimate
from a neighbouring parameter value is therefore admissible, so an
optimiser can pass the sweep of iteration $i-1$ to iteration $i$ and
run one pass rather than two.

The weight is a controller input held in plain \texttt{double}: the
controller is not differentiated, and a weight carried into the
derivative would reintroduce the step-size term above. The
interpolation is linear rather than PCHIP for the same reason and two
more: $\lambda$ jumps where the objective seeds it and where an event
resets the state, and shape preservation is of no value for a weight
whose overshoots cost only time. \texttt{breaks} names the sample
indices an interpolant must not span, and a query inside such an
interval takes the nearer endpoint. A \texttt{floor} raises weights
below a given fraction of the largest, as a precaution rather than a
necessity: $\lambda$ measures a linearised influence, and a state it
weights near zero may still move nonlinearly.

With \texttt{adjointGrid = TRUE} a reverse solve also returns the grid
the sweep ran on, $\lambda$ at the start of each step, and
$\eta_n = \lambda(t_{n+1})^{\mathsf T} e_n$ for each step, the
numerator of \eqref{eq:goal-oriented}. The estimate is of first order,
since it evaluates $\lambda$ at the computed rather than the exact
state; the adaptation needs the ranking of the steps, not the
magnitude.

### Relation to the forward mode

Forward and reverse derivatives of the same model do not agree to
machine precision: with \texttt{sensErrCon = TRUE} the two modes
differentiate different discretisations, each exactly, and the
difference falls with the tolerance. The value and the reverse gradient
returned to the caller are consistent, which a trust-region method,
comparing a predicted with an achieved reduction, relies on.

Of the four methods, the Rosenbrock adjoint is the most accurate: its
stages are direct solves, so its adjoint is the exact transpose of the
discrete step, whereas the adjoint of a corrector applies the implicit
function theorem to an iteration stopped at a finite tolerance.

The reverse mode supports all four methods, time- and root-triggered
events, forcings, the batch entry point and the sparse linear solver.
It is implemented in \texttt{cppde\_adjoint\_step.hpp},
\texttt{cppde\_reverse\_step.hpp} and
\texttt{cppde\_reverse\_trajectory.hpp}.

### Second derivatives: forward over reverse \label{sec:fwdrev}

For a fixed cotangent, \eqref{eq:adjoint-contraction} defines the
gradient map
\begin{equation}
  \bar\theta : \mathbb{R}^{M} \to \mathbb{R}^{M},
  \qquad \theta \mapsto \nabla_\theta J(\theta),
  \label{eq:gradient-map}
\end{equation}
whose Jacobian is the Hessian $\nabla^2_\theta J$. The sweep that
evaluates \eqref{eq:gradient-map} is generic in the scalar type, so
instantiating it on $\mathtt{dual}\langle\mathtt{double}, N\rangle$
instead of \texttt{double} differentiates the sweep itself. Seeded with
a tangent $V \in \mathbb{R}^{M \times N}$ it returns
$(\nabla_\theta J,\; \nabla^2_\theta J\,V)$, both exact rather than
difference quotients [@pearlmutter1994fast]; for $V = I_M$ the second
member is the Hessian. For an ODE this is the second-order adjoint
[@wang1992second; @ozyurt2005cheap]. It is selected by
\texttt{derivMode = "forward-reverse"} and reported as
\verb|curvature|, of shape $[n_x + n_p, N, n_{\text{seed}}]$, beside
the \verb|cotangent| and \verb|tangent| of the same run.

The tangents satisfy the second-order adjoint system. For a direction
$v = (v_0, v_p)$ in $\theta$, let $\sigma$ be the directional
sensitivity and $\mu$ the tangent of $\lambda$ along $v$. Then $\sigma$
solves \eqref{eq:sensitivity-p} contracted with $v$,
\begin{equation}
  \dot\sigma = \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\,\sigma
             + \frac{\partial f}{\partial p}\,v_p,
  \qquad \sigma(t_0) = v_0,
  \label{eq:soa-tangent}
\end{equation}
and differentiating \eqref{eq:adjoint-ode} along $v$ gives $\mu$
backwards from $\mu(T^+) = 0$,
\begin{equation}
  \dot\mu_i = -\sum_k \frac{\partial f_k}{\partial x_i}\,\mu_k
            - \sum_k \lambda_k \left(
                \sum_j \frac{\partial^2 f_k}{\partial x_i\, \partial x_j}\,\sigma_j
              + \sum_m \frac{\partial^2 f_k}{\partial x_i\, \partial p_m}\,v_m
              \right),
  \label{eq:soa-adjoint}
\end{equation}
with jumps $\mu(t_o^-) = \mu(t_o^+) + \dot w_o$, where $\dot w_o$ is
the derivative of the cotangent row $w_o$ along $v$. It is zero for a
cotangent independent of $\theta$; a cotangent formed from the
solution, such as a weighted residual, supplies it through the
\texttt{curvature} argument, an array
$[n_{\mathrm{out}}, n_x, n_{\mathrm{seed}}, N]$. Without it the
gradient is unchanged and the Hessian misses the dependence of the
cotangent on $\theta$. Differentiating \eqref{eq:adjoint-quadrature}
along $v$ gives the two halves of $\nabla^2_\theta J\,v$: the state
half $\mu(t_0)$ and the parameter half
\begin{equation}
  \int_{t_0}^{T}\left(
      \sum_k \frac{\partial f_k}{\partial p_m}\,\mu_k
    + \sum_k \lambda_k \left(
        \sum_j \frac{\partial^2 f_k}{\partial p_m\, \partial x_j}\,\sigma_j
      + \sum_l \frac{\partial^2 f_k}{\partial p_m\, \partial p_l}\,v_l
      \right)\right)\mathrm{d}t .
  \label{eq:soa-quadrature}
\end{equation}
cppDE does not integrate \eqref{eq:soa-tangent} to
\eqref{eq:soa-quadrature} but obtains their discrete counterpart from
the dual instantiation: the tangent carried alongside $\lambda$ is
$\mu$ on the grid the forward run chose, and the tangent of the
parameter accumulator is \eqref{eq:soa-quadrature}. The second
derivatives of $f$ in \eqref{eq:soa-adjoint} and
\eqref{eq:soa-quadrature} come from instantiating the first-order
contractions $J^{\mathsf T}\lambda$ and
$(\partial f/\partial p)^{\mathsf T}\lambda$ over duals, so forward
over reverse needs no generated expression beyond those of the
first-order sweep. For a Rosenbrock method these already include the
contractions of $J v$, which are second derivatives of $f$.

The sweep reads tangents from its checkpoints, so the forward pass is a
sensitivity run in the same $N$ directions. Its error control reads the
values only, so it takes the grid of a value run. The cost, one
sensitivity integration and one sweep, both of width $N$, is linear in
$N$. Forward over forward, selected by
\texttt{derivMode = "forward-forward"} or \texttt{deriv2 = TRUE},
propagates the full second-order sensitivity tensor through the
integration at a cost quadratic in $M$. A difference quotient of the
gradient would cost $N$ further gradient evaluations and lose half of
the available digits.

Forward over forward returns a different object:
\verb|hessian|, the second derivatives of every state with respect to
every pair of parameters, from which the Hessian of any functional can
be contracted afterwards. Forward over reverse returns the Hessian of
one functional. For a likelihood the mixed route is cheaper by a factor
of $M$; where the states themselves are of interest, \verb|hessian| is
the only route.

The second order needs two further facilities. The iteration matrix
carries tangents, so the transposed solve applies the implicit function
theorem with the matrix transposed alongside;
\texttt{cppde\_ad\_lu.hpp} and \texttt{cppde\_sparse\_ad\_lu.hpp}
provide this in the dense and the sparse case. And a generated model
body opens an arena scope of its own, which would release a tangent
allocated there for one of the caller's numbers, so the sweep binds the
tangent storage of every buffer before passing it to the model, as the
stepper does for its own buffers through the tangent slab.

The two second-order routes agree to $10^{-6}$ on \texttt{bdf},
\texttt{rb4} and \texttt{tsit5}, and all four methods return the same
Hessian in reverse to $10^{-5}$. The second comparison is the stronger:
the four methods adapt grids of their own, so agreement means that
each sweep differentiated the discretisation its own method applied.

## Batches of conditions \label{sec:batch}

\texttt{solveODEBatch()} solves $K$ conditions of one model in a single
\texttt{.Call}, in three phases. The main thread reads the arguments of
every condition from R into plain C++ structures. OpenMP threads then
run the $K$ solves with dynamic scheduling, so a slow condition does
not hold up the others; the workers touch neither the R API nor R's
allocator, which is not thread-safe. The main thread finally builds the
result list. When \texttt{times} fixes the output grid, the result
arrays are allocated before the parallel phase and the workers write
into them directly; a root event leaves the row count open until the
solve ends, and its output is copied afterwards.

Each condition is solved as \texttt{solveODE()} would solve it: the
workers share no state and form no reductions across conditions, so the
result is bitwise identical to the serial loop, whatever the thread
count and schedule.

The thread count is the smaller of the request and $K$. It falls to one
inside an enclosing OpenMP region, where the caller already runs in
parallel, and in a child created by \texttt{fork()}, because the OpenMP
thread pool does not survive a fork; a \texttt{pthread\_atfork} handler
marks the child. The BLAS library's own threads are set to one for the
duration of a batch and restored afterwards, and the same handler does
so around every \texttt{fork()}. \texttt{forkGuard()} reports which
BLAS library was found, and \texttt{batchAvailable()} whether a model
