runs its conditions in parallel.

\texttt{prepareBatch()} performs the first phase once and keeps the
converted arguments in a handle; \texttt{solveBatch()} then solves the
same conditions with new parameter values, tangents, cotangents or
error weights of unchanged shapes, as an optimiser does at every
iteration. Reverse-mode solves use the same entry with one cotangent
per condition, and \texttt{cvode()} models provide the same batch
entry.

# \texttt{cvode()} \label{sec:cvode}

\texttt{cvode()} compiles a model against SUNDIALS CVODE/CVODES
($\ge 6.0$), installed on the build host, and exposes it through the
\texttt{solveODE()} interface of \texttt{cppODE()}.

## What is shared

The code generator, the \texttt{events}, \texttt{forcings},
\texttt{rootfunc} and \texttt{fixed} arguments, the returned object and
the column order of \texttt{parms} and \texttt{tangent} are those of
\texttt{cppODE()}. The Jacobian $J = \partial f / \partial x$ is formed
on the expression graph of Section \ref{sec:codegen} and emitted as for
\texttt{cppODE()}, linear tables and loops included. Both backends
select the sparse KLU solver for $n_x \ge 8$ states and a structural
density of $J$ of at most $0.4$, provided SuiteSparse was found at
install time, and dense LAPACK otherwise; \texttt{sparse = TRUE}
requires KLU. Forcing functions are PCHIP interpolants, events reset
the state discontinuously, and root events fire when a user-supplied
scalar function crosses zero. The chain rule
$S_\theta = S_p\,\partial p / \partial \theta$ of
\eqref{eq:sensitivity-theta} is that of \texttt{cppODE()}, with the
same \texttt{tangent} shapes (state-only, full, partial) and row-name
conventions.

## What differs

\textbf{Sensitivity right-hand side.} CVODES integrates the
forward-sensitivity equation
\begin{equation}
  \dot S_k = J(x, p)\, S_k + \frac{\partial f}{\partial p_k},
  \qquad k = 1, \dots, n_p,
  \label{eq:cvodes-sens}
\end{equation}
directly. Its generated right-hand side is one Jacobian-vector product
of $f$ in the direction $(S_k, \partial p/\partial\theta_k)$, evaluated
in \texttt{double} without forming $J$. The in-tree backend obtains the
same equation, \eqref{eq:sensitivity-p}, by evaluating $f$ on
dual-typed state. The generated product avoids the arena allocation of
each dual evaluation but runs once per direction; the dual evaluation
carries all directions in one pass.

\textbf{Methods.} CVODE provides only the multistep families, selected
by \texttt{method = "bdf"} or \texttt{"adams"}; \texttt{rb4} and
\texttt{tsit5} are unavailable. The stability properties of Section
\ref{sec:cppde} apply unchanged.

\textbf{Second-order sensitivities.} CVODES provides only first-order
forward sensitivities, and \texttt{cvode()} does not accept
\texttt{deriv2 = TRUE}.

\textbf{Events.} Events use the Heun transport of \texttt{cppODE()}
with the first-order corrections \eqref{eq:fixed-heun} and
\eqref{eq:dt-star-first}. The transport runs in the generated glue,
outside CVODES, which re-initialises its sensitivities from the
transported state.

## Adjoint sensitivity analysis \label{sec:asa}

\texttt{cvode(..., derivMode = "reverse")} compiles the CVODES adjoint
sensitivity analysis (ASA) in place of forward sensitivities and
returns the \verb|$cotangent| of a native reverse solve: the
contraction \eqref{eq:adjoint-contraction}, states first and
parameters second. The rest of the call, batch entry point included, is
unchanged.

\textbf{Backward problem.} Where \texttt{cppODE()} transposes the
forward steps, CVODES integrates \eqref{eq:adjoint-ode} as an ODE of
its own [@cao2003adjoint]. The generated glue emits both right-hand
sides as vector-Jacobian products of $f$ (Section \ref{sec:codegen}),
the contractions of the native reverse mode, without forming $J$:
\begin{equation}
  \dot\lambda = -\left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\right)^{\!\mathsf T}\!\lambda,
  \qquad
  \dot q = -\left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial p}\right)^{\!\mathsf T}\!\lambda,
  \label{eq:asa-system}
\end{equation}
the second being the quadrature \eqref{eq:adjoint-quadrature} with
$q(T) = 0$. CVODES carries it alongside the backward state and, by
default, leaves it out of the error test: with gradient entries of very
different scale the test would stall the backward step. Both equations run from $T$ down to
$t_0$; the minus signs cancel against the reversed limits, so
$\lambda(t_0)$ is the state part of the gradient and $q(t_0)$ the
parameter part. The backward problem is a BDF solve with the linear
solver of the forward problem, KLU for a sparse model, and the analytic
Jacobian $-J^{\top}$, formed from $J$ in the forward pattern, at the
caller's tolerances and step budget.

\textbf{Checkpoints.} The backward right-hand side needs $x(t)$, which
the forward pass does not keep. CVODES stores a checkpoint every
\texttt{asaCheckpoints} accepted steps, $200$ by default, and recovers
the states between two checkpoints by re-integrating forward from the
earlier one and interpolating; the argument trades memory against
re-integration. This is the main difference between the two
discretisations: the adjoint sees interpolated states, not the ones
the forward run stepped through, so the gradient is the derivative of
no discretisation actually carried out. It approximates the exact
gradient to $O(\mathrm{tol})$ and differs by the same order from the
derivative of the reported value.

\textbf{Jumps at observations.} $\lambda$ starts from the cotangent
row of the last observation, and the sweep stops at each earlier
observation time to add its row, the jump condition of
\eqref{eq:adjoint-ode}. A jump is a new initial condition, so the
backward problem is re-initialised where a row is nonzero, and only
there: re-initialising at every output time would reduce the method to
first order at times the objective does not observe.

\textbf{Several cotangents.} The columns of a cotangent share the
checkpoints, but each needs its own backward integration, where the
native mode sweeps its stored checkpoints once per column. The native
arguments \texttt{keepStore}, \texttt{store}, \texttt{adjointGrid} and
\texttt{errWeights} have no counterpart, since CVODES holds its own
checkpoints and runs its own backward controller.

\textbf{Restrictions.} Events and root functions are rejected at code
generation: a jump in the state implies a jump in $\lambda$, which ASA
cannot apply. The same model cannot also provide forward
sensitivities, and there is no second-order mode. An event model, a
Hessian, or a gradient consistent with the value it accompanies
therefore requires the native backend.

As an independent implementation of the same mathematics, ASA checks
the in-tree adjoint: the two agree to $10^{-6}$ on the test models.

# \texttt{cppFUN()} \label{sec:funcpp}

\texttt{cppFUN()} compiles a system of algebraic expressions
\begin{equation}
  y_i = g_i(x_1, \dots, x_{n_x}, p_1, \dots, p_{n_p}),
  \qquad i = 1, \dots, n_y,
  \label{eq:funcpp}
\end{equation}
with its first and second derivatives and no time integration. The
variables $x$ are the rows of an $n_{\mathrm{obs}} \times n_x$ matrix,
one per observation; the parameters $p$ are shared by all rows. Typical
uses are observation maps, which connect integrator output to data and
whose derivatives enter the gradient of a likelihood, and
reparametrisations $p = \Phi(\theta)$, whose Jacobian is the tangent of
\eqref{eq:sensitivity-theta}.

The expressions are parsed into the expression graph of Section
\ref{sec:codegen}, from which the generator emits one function template
over the scalar type that evaluates $g$ for one observation, instantiated
on \texttt{double}, on \texttt{cppde::dual<double, 0>} and on the nested
dual \texttt{cppde::dual2nd<double, 0>}. The vector-Jacobian product is
a reverse sweep on the same graph, emitted as a second template and
instantiated on \texttt{double} and on the dual.

Every entry runs compiled code. With the default \texttt{compile = FALSE}
the constructor only writes the source; the object must be passed to
\texttt{compile()} before use, and its functions stop with an error
until then.

## Entry points and derivative directions

\texttt{derivMode} names the derivative directions built:
\verb|"forward"|, \verb|"reverse"| or both, the default. Naming one
omits the entries of the other and their compile time. \texttt{deriv}
and \texttt{deriv2} switch the first- and second-order entries;
\texttt{deriv2 = TRUE} requires \verb|"forward"|. Table
\ref{tab:funcpp-dispatch} lists the R functions of the returned object
and the compiled entries they call.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{@{} l l l @{}}
\toprule
R function & direction & compiled entry \\
\midrule
\texttt{func(x, p)}                                            & both    & \texttt{\_eval\_c} \\
\texttt{jac(x, p[, tangentX, tangentP])}                       & forward & \texttt{\_eval\_ad\_c} \\
\texttt{hess(x, p[, tangentX, tangentP, hessianX, hessianP])}  & forward & \texttt{\_eval\_ad2\_c} \\
\texttt{evaluate(\ldots, deriv2)}                              & forward & \texttt{\_eval\_ad\_c} or \texttt{\_eval\_ad2\_c} \\
\texttt{evaluateBatch(sets, cores, deriv2)}                    & forward & \texttt{\_eval\_ad\_batch} or \texttt{\_eval\_ad2\_batch} \\
\texttt{vjp(x, p, cotangent)}                                  & reverse & \texttt{\_vjp\_c} \\
\texttt{vjp(x, p, cotangent, tangentX, tangentP, curvature)}   & reverse & \texttt{\_vjp\_ad\_c} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{R functions of a \texttt{cppFUN()} object and the compiled
entries they call, each prefixed by the model name. The \texttt{\_c}
entries are \texttt{.Call} interfaces that take their arguments by
reference; \texttt{\_eval}, \texttt{\_eval\_ad}, \texttt{\_eval\_ad2} and
\texttt{\_vjp} also exist as \texttt{.C} interfaces, used only for a
shared object without the \texttt{.Call} symbol.}
\label{tab:funcpp-dispatch}
\end{table}

\textbf{Forward direction.} \texttt{jac} evaluates $g$ on duals and
returns $\partial y/\partial\theta$ as an array
$[n_{\mathrm{obs}}, n_y, n_\theta]$; \texttt{hess} evaluates it on
nested duals and returns $\partial^2 y/\partial\theta^2$ as
$[n_{\mathrm{obs}}, n_y, n_\theta, n_\theta]$. The directions $\theta$
are set by the tangents of the next section. Without them the identity
over the variables and the differentiated parameters is used, which
gives the Jacobian or Hessian with respect to $(x, p)$.
\texttt{evaluate} returns value and derivatives from one pass as
\texttt{y}, \texttt{tangent} and, with \texttt{deriv2 = TRUE},
\texttt{hessian}; separate calls of \texttt{func}, \texttt{jac} and
\texttt{hess} would evaluate $g$ up to three times.
\texttt{evaluateBatch} runs \texttt{evaluate} over a list of argument
sets in one call, distributed over OpenMP threads with dynamic
scheduling, and falls back to a loop for fewer than two sets.

\textbf{Reverse direction.} For a cotangent $w$ of the outputs,
$[n_{\mathrm{obs}}, n_y]$ or $[n_{\mathrm{obs}}, n_y, n_{\mathrm{seed}}]$,
\texttt{vjp} returns
\begin{equation}
  (w_x)_{o j s} = \sum_{i} w_{o i s}\,
      \frac{\partial g_i}{\partial x_j}(x_o, p),
  \qquad
  (w_p)_{k s} = \sum_{o} \sum_{i} w_{o i s}\,
      \frac{\partial g_i}{\partial p_k}(x_o, p),
  \label{eq:funcpp-vjp}
\end{equation}
as \texttt{cotangentX} and \texttt{cotangentP}, together with the value
$y$; the parameter part sums over the observations, which share $p$.
The contraction is one reverse sweep per observation and cotangent
column, at a cost independent of the number of upstream parameters, and
forms neither the Jacobian nor the Hessian. Statements of the sweep
that do not depend on the cotangent are evaluated once per observation,
outside the loop over cotangent columns.

Given the tangents $v_x$ and $v_p$ of the inputs in $n_{\mathrm{dir}}$
directions as \texttt{tangentX} and \texttt{tangentP}, or the
derivative $\dot w$ of the cotangent along them as \texttt{curvature},
\texttt{vjp} runs the same template on duals and additionally returns
\begin{equation}
  \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}v}\bigl(w^{\mathsf T} J\bigr)
    = w^{\mathsf T}\,\frac{\partial J}{\partial (x, p)}\,v
      + \dot w^{\mathsf T} J,
  \qquad J = \frac{\partial g}{\partial (x, p)},
  \label{eq:funcpp-vjp-curvature}
\end{equation}
as \texttt{curvatureX} and \texttt{curvatureP}. This is forward over
reverse (Section \ref{sec:fwdrev}): an observation map contributes its
curvature to a backward chain without forming a Hessian.

## Tangent, hessian, cotangent and curvature

A map has a tangent and a Hessian, a functional a cotangent and a
curvature. For the upstream map $\Phi: \theta \mapsto (x, p)$ these are
the \texttt{tangent} $\partial\Phi(\theta)$ and the \texttt{hessian}
$\partial^2\Phi(\theta)$; for a scalar functional $L$ of the outputs
$y$, the \texttt{cotangent} $\partial L(y)$ and the \texttt{curvature}
$\partial^2 L(y)\,\partial y$, the derivative of the cotangent along the
tangent. An argument and its result share a name (Table
\ref{tab:derivative-names}): a forward argument lives on the inputs and
its result on the outputs, a reverse argument on the outputs and its
result on the inputs.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{@{} l l l @{}}
\toprule
\texttt{solveODE()} & \texttt{cppFUN()} argument & \texttt{cppFUN()} result \\
\midrule
\texttt{tangent}   & \texttt{tangentX}, \texttt{tangentP} & \texttt{tangent} \\
\texttt{hessian}   & \texttt{hessianX}, \texttt{hessianP} & \texttt{hessian} \\
\texttt{cotangent} & \texttt{cotangent}                   & \texttt{cotangentX}, \texttt{cotangentP} \\
\texttt{curvature} & \texttt{curvature}                   & \texttt{curvatureX}, \texttt{curvatureP} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Names of the four derivative objects in R. \texttt{solveODE()}
uses one name for the argument and the element of its result; the
\texttt{cppFUN()} results are elements of the lists that
\texttt{evaluate} and \texttt{vjp} return.}
\label{tab:derivative-names}
\end{table}

Forward over forward takes the \texttt{hessian} of the inputs and
returns that of the outputs, the second derivatives of every output in
every pair of tangent directions. Forward over reverse takes the
\texttt{curvature} of the outputs and returns that of the inputs, the
Hessian of the seeded functional applied to the tangent, or, with the
identity tangent, the columns of that Hessian.

\textbf{Chain rule.} \texttt{cppFUN()} takes the tangent and the hessian
of its inputs in two blocks each:
\begin{itemize}
\item \texttt{tangentX[obs, name, theta]}: $\partial x_i/\partial\theta_a$,
per observation row, variable and direction $\theta_a$;
\item \texttt{tangentP[name, theta]}: $\partial p_j/\partial\theta_a$, the
same for all observations;
\item \texttt{hessianX[obs, name, theta1, theta2]}:
$\partial^2 x_i/\partial\theta_a\partial\theta_b$, optional, zero by
default;
\item \texttt{hessianP[name, theta1, theta2]}:
$\partial^2 p_j/\partial\theta_a\partial\theta_b$, optional, zero by
default.
\end{itemize}
They may also be supplied as the attributes \texttt{deriv} and
\texttt{deriv2} of the variables and parameters. Tangent rows of
parameters in \texttt{fixed} are zero, and symbols absent from the
tangent contribute zero.

With the tangent $\partial\Phi \in \mathbb{R}^{n_{\mathrm{obs}} \times
n_{\mathrm{diff}} \times n_\theta}$ over the
$n_{\mathrm{diff}} = n_x + n_p$ inputs and the hessian $\partial^2\Phi$,
the chain rule gives the Jacobian
\begin{equation}
  \frac{\partial y}{\partial\theta}\bigg|_{\mathrm{obs}}
    = J\bigl(x_{\mathrm{obs}}, p\bigr) \cdot \partial\Phi_{\mathrm{obs}},
\end{equation}
and the Hessian of output $o$
\begin{equation}
  \frac{\partial^2 y_o}{\partial\theta\,\partial\theta^\top}\bigg|_{\mathrm{obs}}
    = \partial\Phi_{\mathrm{obs}}^\top \, H_o\bigl(x_{\mathrm{obs}}, p\bigr) \,
      \partial\Phi_{\mathrm{obs}}
    + \sum_{i} J_{o, i}\bigl(x_{\mathrm{obs}}, p\bigr) \,
        \partial^2\Phi_{\mathrm{obs}, i, \cdot, \cdot},
\end{equation}
whose second term vanishes when $\Phi$ is affine.

Neither $J$ nor $H$ is formed: both contractions follow from seeding
the tangent slots of the duals. Each input scalar $x_i$ becomes
\begin{equation*}
  \tilde x_i = (x_i + \partial\Phi_{i,\cdot}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{in}})
             + \bigl(\partial\Phi_{i,\cdot}
                     + \partial^2\Phi_{i,\cdot,\cdot}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{in}}\bigr)\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{out}},
\end{equation*}
a nested dual whose inner tangent slots carry $\partial x_i/\partial\theta$
and whose outer tangent slot $k$ is an inner dual with value
$\partial x_i/\partial\theta_k$ and inner tangents
$\partial^2 x_i/\partial\theta_k\partial\theta$. The multiplication rule
then propagates the $\partial\Phi^\top H\, \partial\Phi$ and
$J \cdot \partial^2\Phi$ terms in one evaluation; the inner tangents of
$\tilde y$ are $\partial y/\partial\theta$, and the cross slots
$\tilde y[k][m]$ are $\partial^2 y/\partial\theta_k\partial\theta_m$.

## Pass-through of unmodelled inputs

With \texttt{attach.input = TRUE}, inputs that do not appear among the
variables and parameters of \eqref{eq:funcpp} are appended to the output
unchanged: their values are copied, their Jacobian rows are zero for a
variable and the identity for a parameter, and their Hessian rows are
zero. An observation map then need not repeat every column of the
integrator output as an identity, as with the partial-shape
\texttt{tangent} of \texttt{solveODE()}.

\clearpage

# Benchmarks \label{sec:bench}

Both backends take the right-hand side, Jacobian, events and
linear-solver choice from the same expression graph and run at the same
tolerances, so a head-to-head measurement compares the numerical cores.

\textbf{Setup.} The suite comprises $43$ problems
(Table \ref{tab:bench-models}): $33$ published systems-biology models
of the PEtab benchmark collection [@hass2019benchmark; @schmiester2021petab]
and $10$ classical test problems, with $n_x = 2$ to $504$ states.
First-order sensitivities run forward for up to $M = 32$ parameters and
in reverse on the two models with $M \ge 120$, Lang and Chen. Both backends use BDF/NDF with the
automatically selected linear solver at
$(\mathrm{rtol}, \mathrm{atol}) \in \{(10^{-4}, 10^{-6}),
(10^{-7}, 10^{-9}), (10^{-10}, 10^{-12})\}$, and a cell reports the
median of five batches of at least $0.25$ s. The suite ran on AMD EPYC
7513 nodes with twelve workers each; both backends of a cell ran in the
same worker. Ratios are geometric means over the three tolerances;
Figure \ref{fig:bench} shows $t_{\texttt{cvode()}} / t_{\texttt{cppODE()}}$
per problem.

\begin{figure}[h]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{fig-speedup.pdf}
\caption{Head-to-head ratio of the two backends, one marker per
problem and mode; above the line \texttt{cppODE()} is faster. The plain
solve is placed at the $M$ of its sensitivity counterpart.}
\label{fig:bench}
\end{figure}

\textbf{Plain solves.} \texttt{cppODE()} is faster on $41$ of $43$
problems, by a geometric mean of $1.15$, with about as many steps as
CVODE (ratios of accepted steps and right-hand-side evaluations $1.02$
and $1.06$). The margin is a cost per step: the model functions are
inlined into the stepper, whereas CVODE calls them through function
pointers and dispatches every vector operation through the
\texttt{N\_Vector} table.

\textbf{Forward sensitivities.} \texttt{cppODE()} is faster on $34$ of
$41$ problems, by $1.29$, and the ratio grows with $M$: $1.01$ for
$M \le 3$, $1.22$ for $4 \le M \le 12$ and $1.52$ for
$13 \le M \le 32$. CVODES evaluates one Jacobian-vector product per
parameter; the in-tree backend evaluates $f$ once on a dual state that
carries all $M$ tangents and needs about one eleventh of the
right-hand-side evaluations. The dual evaluation has a cost per state
component independent of $M$, so problems with few parameters fall
below parity: six of the seven slower ones have $M \le 6$, the lowest
being Salazar-Cavazos ($n_x = 75$, $M = 6$) at $0.67$.

\textbf{Reverse sensitivities.} Measured in plain solves, the cost of one
gradient by forward sensitivities is linear in $M$
(Figure \ref{fig:gradient}):
$1.8 + 0.60\,M$ for \texttt{cppODE()} and $1.2 + 0.84\,M$ for CVODES,
about $92$ and $129$ at $M = 152$. The discrete adjoint of
Section \ref{sec:reverse} costs $6.3$ plain solves on Chen and
$3.6$ on Lang, independent of $M$. The CVODES
adjoint of Section \ref{sec:asa}, which does not support the events
of Chen, costs $27$ plain CVODE solves on Lang and takes $8.8$ to
$13.7$ times as long as the discrete adjoint.

\begin{figure}[h]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{fig-gradient.pdf}
\caption{Cost of one gradient by forward sensitivities in units of the
plain solve of the same problem and backend, with least-squares lines.}
\label{fig:gradient}
\end{figure}

A separate run on the six models with $M \ge 40$, one core per model,
compares the two adjoints directly (Figure \ref{fig:adjoint}). The
CVODES adjoint takes $8.7$ to $18.8$ times as long on Lang,
Lucarelli and Raim\'undez, and $1.0$ to $1.5$
times on Zheng ($n_x = 15$), where a solve takes about a
millisecond. The discrete adjoint runs backward over the steps of the
forward solve, whereas CVODES chooses its own backward steps and
recomputes the forward state between checkpoints. At
$\mathrm{rtol} = 10^{-10}$ both gradients deviate from the reference by
$10^{-10}$ to $5 \cdot 10^{-7}$.

\begin{figure}[h]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{fig-adjoint.pdf}
\caption{Time of one gradient by the CVODES adjoint over the time by the
discrete adjoint, per model and tolerance; right of the line the
discrete adjoint is faster.}
\label{fig:adjoint}
\end{figure}

\textbf{Second order.} The Hessian of the summed outputs is measured for
\texttt{cppODE()} alone, on models with at most $30$ states: forward over
reverse (Section \ref{sec:fwdrev}) with up to $32$ directions, forward
over forward up to $10$ states and $10$ directions. Fitted in log-log,
the cost grows with exponent $1.9$ forward over forward and $0.6$
forward over reverse (Figure \ref{fig:hessian}). The two break even at
$M = 3$; forward over reverse is $3.0$ times faster at $M = 6$ and $9$
to $14$ times at $M = 9$ and $10$. At $\mathrm{rtol} = 10^{-10}$ the
Hessians deviate from the forward-over-forward Hessian at the reference
tolerance by a median of $8.1 \cdot 10^{-10}$ (forward over forward)
and $1.8 \cdot 10^{-8}$ (forward over reverse).

\begin{figure}[h]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{fig-hessian.pdf}
\caption{Cost of one Hessian of the summed outputs in units of the
plain solve. The lines are power laws fitted in log-log over $M > 1$.}
\label{fig:hessian}
\end{figure}

\begin{figure}[!b]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.5\textwidth]{fig-sparse.pdf}
\caption{Gain of the sparse over the dense linear solver, one marker
per model and backend.}
\label{fig:sparse}
\end{figure}

\textbf{Linear solver.} Seventeen models were solved again with the
linear solver pinned to dense and to sparse. The sparse gain is the
same for both backends and grows from $1.09$ at $n_x = 8$ to $3.3$ at
$n_x = 504$ (Figure \ref{fig:sparse}); the automatic selection chose
the sparse path in every case.

\textbf{Accuracy.} Against a reference at $\mathrm{atol} = 10^{-14}$,
$\mathrm{rtol} = 10^{-12}$ the error of \texttt{cppODE()} is a median
$0.99$ times that of CVODE without sensitivities (central $90\,\%$ of
the problems between $0.51$ and $1.51$) and $1.09$ with sensitivities
(between $0.66$ and $2.37$). The reference is itself a CVODE solution,
which favours CVODE.

\textbf{Failures.} Six of the $1083$ cells failed, all at
$\mathrm{rtol} = 10^{-10}$: the forward sensitivities of
\texttt{cppODE()} on Oliveira with each linear solver and on Weber, and forward over forward
on the same two models.

# BDF and NDF coefficients

\label{app:bdf-coeffs}

\emph{Source.} Shampine and Reichelt [@MATLABODESuite, Table 1]; implemented in
\texttt{cppde\_multistepper.hpp}.

The NDF of order $q$ adds to the BDF$q$ corrector a term proportional
to the Nordsieck predictor error,
\[
  \sum_{m=1}^{q} \frac{1}{m}\, \nabla^{m} x_n
  \;-\; h_n\, f(x_n, t_n)
  \;-\; \kappa_q\, \gamma_q\, \bigl(x_n - x_n^{\mathrm{pred}}\bigr)
  \;=\; 0,
  \qquad
  \gamma_q \;=\; \sum_{m=1}^{q} \tfrac{1}{m}.
\]
Setting $\kappa_q = 0$ recovers BDF$q$. Table \ref{tab:ndf-kappa}
lists the $\kappa_q$ of cppDE with the step-size gain over BDF$q$ and
the stability angle. The argument \texttt{useNDF} (default
\texttt{TRUE}) selects NDF or BDF at compile time.

\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{@{} c S[table-format=-1.4] l l @{}}
\toprule
$q$ & {$\kappa_q$} & Step-size gain over BDF$q$ & Stability angle \\
\midrule
1 & -0.1850 & $+26\,\%$ & A-stable           \\
2 & -0.1111 & $+26\,\%$ & A-stable           \\
3 & -0.0823 & $+26\,\%$ & $80^\circ$         \\
4 & -0.0415 & $+12\,\%$ & $66^\circ$         \\
5 &  0.0000 & $0\,\%$   & $51^\circ$ ($=$ BDF5) \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{NDF correction coefficients $\kappa_q$ adopted by cppDE,
the empirical step-size gain over classical BDF$q$ at matched
local error, and the resulting stability angle.}
\label{tab:ndf-kappa}
\end{table}

NDF5 is BDF5 ($\kappa_5 = 0$), because the BDF5 stability angle of
$51^\circ$ leaves no room for further reduction.

# Adams-Moulton coefficients

\label{app:adams-coeffs}

\emph{Source.} Hindmarsh et al. [@hindmarsh2005sundials], the
$\ell$-vector formulation of CVODE; implemented in \texttt{adams\_set\_coefficients()} in
\texttt{cppde\_multistepper.hpp}.

The Adams-Moulton coefficients depend on the step-size history, so no
static table holds them: they are recomputed every step from the
Nordsieck array. With $\xi_j = (t_n - t_{n-j})/h_n$, the recurrence
\[
  \ell_0(q) \;=\; 1,
  \qquad
  \ell_j(q) \;=\; \ell_{j-1}(q) \;+\; \xi_j^{-1},
  \qquad j = 1, \dots, q,
\]
followed by a polynomial expansion, yields the corrector weights
$\beta_0, \dots, \beta_q$ of the current step. For
$h_n = h_{n-1} = \cdots$ they reduce to the fixed-step values of
Hairer, N\o{}rsett and Wanner [@hairer2008solving, Table III.1.1].

The maximum order is $q_{\max} = 12$, the CVODE default; the order
controller selects $q \in \{1, \dots, 12\}$ at run time.

# Rosenbrock4 coefficients

\label{app:ros-coeffs}

\emph{Source.} Hairer and Wanner [@hairer2010solving, §IV.7], identical to the default
coefficients of the \texttt{rosenbrock4} stepper of
Boost.Numeric.Odeint; implemented in
\texttt{default\_rosenbrock\_coefficients} in
\texttt{cppde\_rosenbrock4.hpp}.

With iteration matrix $W = (\gamma h_n)^{-1} I - J(x_n, t_n)$, a
Rosenbrock method of $s$ stages with diagonal coefficient $\gamma$ has
the stage equations
\begin{align*}
W\, k_i
  &\;=\; f\!\left(x_n + \sum_{j<i} \alpha_{ij}\, k_j,\;
                 t_n + c_i\, h_n \right)
        \;+\; \frac{1}{h_n} \sum_{j<i} \frac{\gamma_{ij}}{\gamma}\, k_j
        \;+\; h_n\, d_i\, \frac{\partial f}{\partial t}, \\
x_{n+1}      &\;=\; x_n + \sum_{i=1}^{s} m_i\, k_i,
   \qquad
\hat x_{n+1} \;=\; x_n + \sum_{i=1}^{s} \hat m_i\, k_i.
\end{align*}
cppDE uses $s = 6$ and $\gamma = 1/4$. The tables are indexed as in
the source code: $\gamma$, the time partials and the node positions in
Table \ref{tab:ros-diag}, the stage couplings in Tables
\ref{tab:ros-alpha} and \ref{tab:ros-gamma}, the sixth-row weights in
Table \ref{tab:ros-weights} and the dense-output coefficients in
Table \ref{tab:ros-dense}.

\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{@{} c S @{\quad} c S @{\quad} c S @{}}
\toprule
$\gamma$ & {0.25} & $d_1$ & {0.25}    & $c_2$ & {0.386} \\
$d_2$    & {-0.1043} & $d_3$ & {0.1035} & $c_3$ & {0.21}  \\
$d_4$    & {0.0362}  &       &           & $c_4$ & {0.63}  \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Rosenbrock4 diagonal coefficient $\gamma$, time-partial
coefficients $d_i$, and stage node positions $c_i$.}
\label{tab:ros-diag}
\end{table}

# Tsitouras 5(4) coefficients

\label{app:tsit5-coeffs}

\emph{Source.} Tsitouras [@TSITOURAS2011770, Table 1 and eqs. (7), (8)];
implemented in \texttt{cppde\_tsit5.hpp}.

The Tsitouras 5(4) pair (Table \ref{tab:tsit5-butcher}) has $s = 7$
stages and satisfies the first column simplifying assumption
$\sum_i b_i a_{ij} = b_j(1 - c_j)$ for every $j$, but not the row
condition $\sum_j a_{ij} c_j = c_i^2/2$. The seventh stage is the FSAL
stage: the row $a_{7,j}$ of the $A$ matrix coincides with $b_j$ for
$j = 1, \dots, 6$.

\centering
\small
\setlength{\tabcolsep}{4pt}

                   S[table-format=1.10] S[table-format=-1.10] S[table-format=-1.10]
                   S[table-format=1.10] @{}}
\toprule
$i$ & {$c_i$} & {$a_{i1}$} & {$a_{i2}$} & {$a_{i3}$} & {$a_{i4}$} & {$a_{i5}$} & {$a_{i6}$} \\
\midrule
1 & 0            &               &                &              &               &               & \\
2 & 0.161        & 0.161         &                &              &               &               & \\
3 & 0.327        & -0.0084806555 & 0.3354806555   &              &               &               & \\
4 & 0.9          & 2.8971530571  & -6.3594484900  & 4.3622954329 &               &               & \\
5 & 0.9800255409 & 5.3258648284  & -11.7488835641 & 7.4955393429 & -0.0924950664 &               & \\
6 & 1.0          & 5.8614554429  & -12.9209693178 & 8.1593678986 & -0.0715849733 & -0.0282690504 & \\
7 & 1.0          & 0.0964607668  & 0.01           & 0.4798896504 & 1.3790085741  & -3.2900695154 & 2.3247105241 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Tsitouras 5(4) nodes $c_i$ and coefficients $a_{ij}$. Row $7$
equals the order-$5$ weights $b_j$ (FSAL).}
\label{tab:tsit5-butcher}
\end{table}

The seventh stage $k_7 = f(x_{n+1},\, t_n + h_n)$ is reused as $k_1$
of step $n+1$. Since $b_7 = 0$ and $\hat b_7 \neq 0$, it enters the
embedded order-$4$ estimate but not the order-$5$ solution. The step
controller uses the local-error estimate
\[
  e_n \;=\; h_n \sum_{i=1}^{7} (\hat b_i - b_i)\, k_i.
\]
Table \ref{tab:tsit5-err} lists the weights and their differences.
